knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit quartic and sextic minimum-volume sublevel sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The prescribed set \(K\) and problem \(\mathbf P\) retain their definitions from the surrounding formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[g_4(x)=x_1^4+x_2^4-x_1^2x_2^2,\qquad G_1^4=\{x:g_4(x)\leq1\},\] and \[g_6(x)=x_1^6+x_2^6-\tfrac12\bigl(x_1^4x_2^2+x_1^2x_2^4\bigr),\qquad G_1^6=\{x:g_6(x)\leq1\}.\] Then \(G_1^4\) is the unique solution of problem \(\mathbf P\) for \(d=4\): \(K\subset G_1^4\), and \(G_1^4\) has minimum volume among the sets containing \(K\) that are defined by homogeneous polynomials of degree four. Likewise, \(G_1^6\) is the unique solution of \(\mathbf P\) for \(d=6\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed quartic and sextic homogeneous polynomials define the unique optimal containing sublevel sets for the surrounding minimum-volume problem in degrees four and six, respectively.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ and }\mathbf P\text{ are those defined in the surrounding minimum-volume containing-sublevel-set formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_1^4\text{ is the unique solution of }\mathbf P\text{ for }d=4,\qquad G_1^6\text{ is the unique solution of }\mathbf P\text{ for }d=6

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent finite-dimensional convex formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The problems \(\mathbf P\) and \(\mathcal P\), and the polynomial class \(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d\), retain their definitions from the surrounding formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g^*\in\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d\), \(g^*\) is an optimal solution of problem \(\mathbf P\) if and only if it is an optimal solution of the associated problem \(\mathcal P\). Moreover, \(\mathcal P\) is a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original polynomial sublevel-set problem and its associated finite-dimensional convex formulation have the same optimizers.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ and }\mathcal P\text{ are the paired problems defined in the surrounding formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^*\in\operatorname{argmin}\mathbf P\iff g^*\in\operatorname{argmin}\mathcal P,\qquad \mathcal P\text{ is finite-dimensional and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, uniqueness, and contact-measure optimality conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the convex problem \(\mathcal P\) defined in the surrounding polynomial sublevel-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact with nonempty interior. Then \(\mathcal P\) has a unique optimal solution \(g^*\in\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d\). If \(g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\), there exists \(\mu^*\in\mathcal M(K)_+\) such that, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb N^n\) with \(|\alpha|=d\), \[\int_{\mathbb R^n}x^\alpha e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx=\int_Kx^\alpha\,d\mu^*,\] and \[\int_K(1-g^*)\,d\mu^*=0,\qquad \mu^*(K)=\frac nd\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx.\] The measure is supported on \(V=\{x\in K:g^*(x)=1\}\) and may be replaced by a positive measure supported on at most \(\binom{n+d-1}{d}\) points of \(V\). Conversely, if \(g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\), \(1-g^*\in C_d(K)\), and there are \(x(i)\in K\) and \(\lambda_i>0\) satisfying \(g^*(x(i))=1\) and \[\int_{\mathbb R^n}x^\alpha e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^s\lambda_i x(i)^\alpha\qquad(|\alpha|=d),\] then \(g^*\) is the unique optimal solution of \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compact K with nonempty interior, the convex sublevel-set problem has a unique optimizer. An interior optimizer has a positive contact-measure certificate matching all degree-d moments, and the certificate can use at most binomial(n+d−1,d) contact points. Conversely, feasible positive contact weights satisfying those moment equations certify unique optimality.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is the convex problem defined in the surrounding formulation}
g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\text{ for the contact-measure conclusion}
g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d),\ 1-g^*\in C_d(K),\ g^*(x(i))=1,\ \lambda_i>0\text{ for the converse}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ has a unique optimizer; under the stated interior condition it admits the displayed contact-measure certificate, and the stated finite contact-point conditions imply unique optimality}

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained global minimization of a real polynomial in one scalar variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[t]\), the univariate unconstrained polynomial model has extended-real optimal value \[p^*:=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}p(t).\] The model is bounded below exactly when \(p^*>-\infty\). In that case the infimum is attained and the nonempty solution set is \[X^*:=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:p(t)=p^*\}.\] Otherwise \(p^*=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a real polynomial over the entire real line. Its infimum is either negative infinity or a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}p(t)\), with attainment whenever \(p^*>-\infty\)

notation.meaning: extended-real global infimum of the polynomial
set of global minimizers when the polynomial is bounded below

knowledge_statements.title: Multivariate Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained global minimization of a real polynomial in finitely many variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the multivariate unconstrained polynomial model is \[f^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x).\] Its global minimizers form \(X^*:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)=f^*\}\) when \(f^*\) is finite and attained. No convexity, coercivity, or boundedness assumption is implicit in this problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a real multivariate polynomial over all Euclidean space, without assuming convexity, boundedness, or attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling classification for unconstrained minimization of a homogeneous polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be homogeneous of positive degree \(d\), so \(f(\lambda x)=\lambda^d f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&f(x)\geq0\text{ for all }x,\\-\infty,&f(u)<0\text{ for some }u.\end{cases}\] In the first case the origin is a global minimizer; in the second, \(f(\lambda u)\to-\infty\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-degree homogeneity forces the unconstrained infimum to be zero for a nonnegative form and negative infinity if any negative value exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\in\{0,-\infty\}\), classified by global nonnegativity

notation.meaning: a point at which the polynomial is negative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT triplet and associated shifted Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT definition for polynomial inequality and equality constraints, using the source's sign convention and subtraction of the global optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A triplet (x^*,\lambda^*,v^*)\in K	imes\mathbb R^{m_1}	imes\mathbb R^{m_2} is a KKT triplet if 
abla f(x^*)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_1}\lambda_j^*
abla g_j(x^*)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_2}v_\ell^*
abla h_\ell(x^*), \lambda_j^*g_j(x^*)=0, and \lambda_j^*\ge0 for every j. Its associated Lagrangian is L(x,\lambda^*,v^*)=f(x)-f^*-\sum_{j=1}^{m_1}\lambda_j^*g_j(x)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_2}v_\ell^*h_\ell(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and multiplier vectors form a KKT triplet when stationarity, complementary slackness, and nonnegativity of inequality multipliers hold. The associated shifted Lagrangian subtracts the optimal value and the multiplier-weighted constraints from the objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Constrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization over the common real zero set of finitely many polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), define the equality-constrained feasible set \[V_{\mathbb{R}}(h):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_j(x)=0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}.\] The associated polynomial optimization model is \[f^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)\}.\] Under the extended-real convention, \(f^*=+\infty\) when \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a polynomial over the real common zero set of finitely many polynomial equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\)

notation.meaning: common real zero set of the equality polynomials

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-Constrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization over a basic closed set defined solely by polynomial inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), define \[K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r\}.\] The inequality-constrained polynomial model is \[f^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in K\}.\] This convention includes no implicit compactness or constraint qualification, and assigns \(f^*=+\infty\) when \(K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a polynomial over a set defined by finitely many non-strict polynomial inequalities, without implicit compactness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Equality–Inequality Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization with simultaneous polynomial equations and non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For polynomials \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m,g_1,\ldots,g_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), let \[K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ g_i(x)\geq0\ (i=1,\ldots,r)\}.\] The mixed equality–inequality polynomial model is \[f^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in K\}.\] Empty constraint families are allowed, recovering the equality-only, inequality-only, and unconstrained subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a polynomial subject simultaneously to finitely many polynomial equalities and non-strict polynomial inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Real Polynomial Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential feasibility for a finite system of real polynomial equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), real polynomial feasibility asks whether \[V_{\mathbb{R}}(h):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_1(x)=\cdots=h_m(x)=0\}\] is nonempty. A feasible certificate in the direct existential sense is any \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(h_j(x^*)=0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether finitely many real polynomial equations possess a common real solution; any common solution directly witnesses feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)\neq\varnothing\) or \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\varnothing\)

notation.meaning: real variety defined by the polynomial equations

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Real Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global polynomial optimization restricted to an algebraic set of real points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_1,\ldots,h_m,f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and let \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_j(x)=0\text{ for all }j\}\). Optimization over the real variety is \[f^*:=\inf_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x).\] The variety may be empty, noncompact, reducible, or positive-dimensional; consequently the extended-real infimum need not be finite or attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a polynomial over the real points satisfying a finite family of polynomial equations, with no compactness or dimensionality assumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\)

notation.meaning: real variety defining the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Finite Real Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and enumeration characterization when the real variety has finitely many points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and suppose the real variety \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\{v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(N)}\}\) is nonempty and finite. Then the polynomial optimization problem over this variety attains its minimum and \[f^*=\min_{1\leq k\leq N}f\bigl(v^{(k)}\bigr),\qquad X^*=\left\{v^{(k)}:f\bigl(v^{(k)}\bigr)=f^*\right\}.\] Thus the optimizer set is also nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty finite real variety, every polynomial attains its minimum, obtained by comparing its values at all feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min_{v\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(v)\) and \(X^*\neq\varnothing\)

notation.meaning: the kth point of the finite real variety

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Closed Semialgebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization over one conjunction of finitely many non-strict polynomial inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) and \(r\geq0\) be integers, and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A basic closed semialgebraic set is a set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) admitting a presentation \[K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r\}.\] When \(r=0\), the conjunction is vacuous and \(K=\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the corresponding optimization model has value \[f^*:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x).\] A polynomial equality may be encoded by a pair of opposite non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic closed model minimizes a polynomial over one finite conjunction of non-strict polynomial inequalities; an empty conjunction gives the whole decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,r\}\) and \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\)

notation.meaning: extended-real optimal value over the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Semialgebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive presentation by finitely many basic closed semialgebraic components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1,\ldots,K_s\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be basic closed semialgebraic sets with \(K_\ell=\{x:g_{\ell i}(x)\geq0, i=1,\ldots,r_\ell\}\). A finite-union model has feasible set \[K=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{s}K_\ell.\] For any polynomial \(f\), its optimal value decomposes as \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=\min_{1\leq\ell\leq s}\inf_{x\in K_\ell}f(x),\] using extended-real infima and assuming \(s\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-union model uses finitely many basic closed components; its infimum is the smallest componentwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\cup_{\ell=1}^sK_\ell}f(x)=\min_{1\leq\ell\leq s}\inf_{x\in K_\ell}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Semialgebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible sets represented by existentially eliminating auxiliary variables from polynomial constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projected semialgebraic model in variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) introduces auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\) and polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_r,h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]\), with feasible set \[S:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\ g_i(x,y)\geq0\ \forall i,\ h_j(x,y)=0\ \forall j\}.\] For a polynomial objective \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x]\), the associated value is \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected model defines feasible decisions by the existence of auxiliary variables satisfying finitely many polynomial equations and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x:\exists y,\ g_i(x,y)\geq0\ \forall i,\ h_j(x,y)=0\ \forall j\}\)

notation.meaning: projected feasible set in decision space

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:K\to\mathbb{R}\) is a piecewise-polynomial objective if there are finitely many semialgebraic sets \(K_1,6fldots,K_m\) covering \(K\) and polynomials \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) such that \(f(x)=p_j(x)\) for every \(x\in K_j\). When the pieces overlap, the defining polynomials satisfy \(p_i(x)=p_j(x)\) on \(K_i\cap K_j\). The associated model is \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-polynomial objective agrees with a polynomial on each member of a finite semialgebraic cover, with coincident values on overlaps.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Polynomial Objectives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence, finite exactness, and extraction for rational moment–SOS relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of relaxations (10.3) and (10.4) in the referenced rational-minimization setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf K\) be as in (5.2), let Assumption 2.14 hold, and consider the semidefinite relaxations (10.3) and (10.4). Then:

(a) \(\rho^*\) is finite and
\[
\rho_d^*\uparrow\rho^*,\qquad \rho_d\uparrow\rho^*\quad\text{as }d\to\infty.
\]

(b) If additionally \(\operatorname{int}(\mathbf K)\neq\varnothing\), then \(\rho_d^*=\rho_d\) for every \(d\).

(c) Let \(\mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\) be a global minimizer of \(p/q\). If the polynomial \(p-\rho^*q\), which is nonnegative on \(\mathbf K\), has Putinar's representation (2.10), then problems (10.3) and (10.4) have optimal solutions, and for some \(d_0\in\mathbb N\),
\[
\rho_d^*=\rho_d=\rho^*\qquad\forall d\ge d_0.
\]

(d) If an optimal solution \(\mathbf y^*\) of (10.3) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_{d-v}(\mathbf y^*)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_d(\mathbf y^*)=s,
\qquad v=\max_j v_j,
\]
then there are \(s\) global minimizers, and they can be extracted by Algorithm 6.9.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced assumptions, both relaxation-value sequences increase to the finite rational optimum. If K has nonempty interior, their values agree at every order. If the optimality-gap polynomial has the stated Putinar representation, the relaxation problems attain optimal solutions and become exact from some finite order onward. An optimal moment solution satisfying the stated flat-rank condition yields s extractable global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\text{ is a global minimizer and }p-\rho^*q\text{ has Putinar's representation (2.10) for clause (c)}
\mathbf y^*\text{ is optimal for (10.3) and }\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_{d-v}(\mathbf y^*)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_d(\mathbf y^*)=s\text{ for clause (d)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_d^*\uparrow\rho^*,\quad\rho_d\uparrow\rho^*,\quad\text{together with clauses (b)--(d) under their respective additional hypotheses}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(q>0\) on \(\mathbf K\), then the optimal value \(\rho^*\) of problem (10.1) equals
\[
\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal M(\mathbf K)_+}\left\{\int_{\mathbf K}p\,d\mu:\int_{\mathbf K}q\,d\mu=1\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If q is strictly positive on K, the optimal value of the rational minimization problem equals the infimum of the integral of p over nonnegative measures on K whose integral of q is one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-Hierarchy Convergence and Rank-Based Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to hierarchy (10.10), retaining the source definitions of \(I_i\), \(s_i\), and \(U_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf K\subset\mathbb R^n\) in (5.2) be compact, and suppose \((I_i)_{i=1}^s\) satisfies the running intersection property (2.27). For hierarchy (10.10), \(f_d^*\uparrow f^*\) as \(d\to\infty\). Moreover, if an optimal solution \(\mathbf y^*=(\mathbf y_1^*,\ldots,\mathbf y_s^*)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^*,I_i)=\operatorname{rank}M_{d-s_i}(\mathbf y_i^*,I_i)=R_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,s\), and \(\operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^*,I_i\cap I_j)=1\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,s-1\) and \(j\in U_i\), then \(f_d^*=f^*\), and finitely many global minimizers can be extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compact rational-sum problems with running-intersection sparsity, the sparse SDP bounds increase to the global optimum. Flat local moment matrices and rank-one overlap matrices imply finite exactness and permit extraction of finitely many global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \text{For finite exactness, }\mathbf y^*\text{ is optimal for (10.10)}
\text{For finite exactness, }\forall i=1,\ldots,s-1,\ \forall j\in U_i,\ \operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^*,I_i\cap I_j)=1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_d^*\uparrow f^*\text{ as }d\to\infty;\quad\text{under the stated rank conditions, }f_d^*=f^*\text{ and finitely many global minimizers can be extracted}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence and Flat-Rank Recovery for the Rational-Sum Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the semidefinite hierarchy (10.8); Assumption 2.14, \(v\), and the moment sequences retain their source definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Assumption 2.14 holds for the polynomials \((g_j)\) defining \(\mathbf K\). For the semidefinite relaxations (10.8), \(f_d^*\uparrow f^*\) as \(d\to\infty\). Moreover, let \((\mathbf y_i^d)_{i=1}^s\) be optimal and satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^d)=\operatorname{rank}M_{d-v}(\mathbf y_i^d)=R\) for every \(i\). If \(R>1\), each corresponding truncated moment sequence has a representing measure supported on \(R\) points \(\mathbf x^\ell(i)\in\mathbf K\). If additionally \(\mathbf x^\ell(i)=\mathbf x^\ell(j)\) for all \(i\ne j\) and every \(\ell\), then \(f_d^*=f^*\), and all those points are global minimizers of \(\mathbf P\). If \(R=1\), then \(f_d^*=f^*\) and \(\mathbf x(i)=\mathbf x^*\) for every \(i\), where \(\mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\) is a global minimizer of \(\mathbf P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Assumption 2.14, the SDP bounds increase to the global optimum. A common flat-rank condition gives finitely atomic representing measures; aligned atoms yield finite exactness and global minimizers, while rank one yields a common global minimizer and finite exactness.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the recovery conclusions, }(\mathbf y_i^d)_{i=1}^s\text{ is optimal for (10.8)}
\text{For the recovery conclusions, }\forall i,\ \operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^d)=\operatorname{rank}M_{d-v}(\mathbf y_i^d)=R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_d^*\uparrow f^*;\quad R>1\Rightarrow\text{the stated atomic-measure conclusion and, under aligned supports, finite exactness and minimizer recovery};\quad R=1\Rightarrow f_d^*=f^*\text{ and }\mathbf x(i)=\mathbf x^*\ \forall i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate polynomial minimization over finitely many nondegenerate compact interval components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\), and let \(K=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}[a_j,b_j]\), where \(m\ge 1\) and \(a_j<b_j<a_{j+1}\) for \(j<m\). Polynomial optimization over a finite union of intervals is the problem \[p^*=\min\{p(x):x\in K\}=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in[a_j,b_j]}p(x).\] Compactness of \(K\) ensures that every component minimum and the global minimum are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a polynomial over finitely many disjoint nondegenerate compact intervals reduces to taking the smallest attained componentwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in[a_j,b_j]}p(x)\), and a minimizer exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Sets of Isolated Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate polynomial minimization on a finite discrete feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\), and let \(K=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\}\subset\mathbb R\) contain distinct points, with \(m\ge 1\). Polynomial optimization on a finite set of isolated points is \[p^*=\min_{x\in K}p(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}p(\xi_i).\] Every feasible point is isolated in the relative topology, and the complete enumeration of the displayed polynomial values produces a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite set of distinct feasible points, global polynomial optimization is exactly comparison of the finitely many objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\min_{1\le i\le m}p(\xi_i)\), attained by at least one \(\xi_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Interval–Point Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate polynomial minimization over nondegenerate interval components and additional isolated points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\), let \(m,r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfy \(m+r\ge1\), and define \(I=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}[a_j,b_j]\) and \(F=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r\}\), with an empty union or set when its index count is zero. When \(m\ge1\), assume \(a_j<b_j<a_{j+1}\) for \(j<m\); when \(r\ge1\), assume the points \(\xi_i\) are distinct and lie outside \(I\). For \(K=I\cup F\), \[\min_{x\in K}p(x)=\min\left(\left\{\min_{x\in[a_j,b_j]}p(x):1\le j\le m\right\}\cup\left\{p(\xi_i):1\le i\le r\right\}\right).\] The minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty union of finitely many nondegenerate compact intervals and finitely many additional isolated points, the global minimum is the smallest interval minimum or isolated-point value.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r\}\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus I\) has distinct elements when \(r\ge1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum over \(K=I\cup F\) is the minimum of the nonempty finite collection of interval minima and isolated-point values, and it is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected-Component Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise characterization of local and global minima on disconnected feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}K_j\subset\mathbb R\), where the nonempty compact sets \(K_j\) are pairwise disjoint and have positive mutual distance, and let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\). Then \[\min_{x\in K}p(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in K_j}p(x).\] Moreover, any point minimizing \(p\) on one component \(K_j\) is a local minimizer relative to \(K\), but it is globally minimizing on \(K\) only when its value equals the smallest component minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated components create relative local minima componentwise, while global optimality requires comparing the minimum values across every component.
assumptions_latex: \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\) are nonempty compact sets with positive pairwise distance
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global minimization is componentwise comparison; a component minimizer need not minimize over all of \(K\).

notation.meaning: connected or disconnected compact feasible components

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical unconstrained quadratic minimization and its finite-optimum criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), a vector \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), an unconstrained quadratic model is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q(x),\qquad q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha.\] Its infimum is finite exactly when \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\). Under these conditions, the minimizers are precisely the solutions of \(Qx=-c\); otherwise the infimum is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained quadratic has a finite minimum exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite and its linear term lies in the Hessian range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf q> -\infty\) iff \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\); then \(\operatorname*{argmin}q=\{x:Qx=-c\}\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical QCQP with a quadratic objective and finitely many quadratic inequality or equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i(x)\le0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\qquad e_j(x)=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,r,\] where \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\) and \(e_j(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}R_jx+d_j^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_j\), with \(Q_i,R_j\in\mathbb S^n\). A standard convex QCQP subclass is obtained when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and every equality function \(e_j\) is affine, equivalently \(R_j=0\). Outside such conditions, a QCQP may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP optimizes a quadratic objective subject to finitely many quadratic inequalities and equalities. Positive-semidefinite objective and inequality Hessians together with affine equalities define the standard convex subclass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed model is a QCQP; \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and \(R_j=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,r\) define its standard convex subclass.

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian matrices of the corresponding quadratic functions

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblems and generalized one-quadratic-constraint variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\), the classical trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad \lVert x\rVert_2\le\Delta.\] The matrix \(Q\) may be indefinite. A generalized trust-region model replaces the ball constraint by \(x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\le0\), where \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The classical feasible ball is nonempty and compact, so its continuous quadratic objective attains a global minimum. This compactness conclusion does not automatically extend to the generalized constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical trust-region problem minimizes a possibly indefinite quadratic over a Euclidean ball and always attains its minimum. A generalized variant uses one quadratic inequality, whose feasible set need not be compact.
assumptions_latex: For the generalized variant, \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The classical trust-region problem has an attained global minimizer even when \(Q\) is indefinite.

notation.meaning: coefficients of the generalized quadratic constraint

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Quadratic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic optimization over the standard simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard quadratic optimization problem associated with \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) is \[p^*=\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx:x\in\Delta_n\},\qquad \Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x=1\}.\] Because \(\Delta_n\) is nonempty and compact, the minimum is attained. The model is generally nonconvex when \(Q\) is not positive semidefinite on the affine hull of the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard quadratic optimization minimizes a quadratic form over the standard simplex; compactness guarantees attainment even when the objective is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\min_{x\in\Delta_n}x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) exists and is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment in convex polynomial optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of a finite real optimal value for a convex polynomial over a convex basic semialgebraic feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge 0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). Suppose that \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\) and each \(-g_j\) are convex. If \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R\), then there exists \(x^*\in K\) such that \(f(x^*)=f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex polynomial program, every finite real infimum is attained by a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in K\quad f(x^*)=f^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SOS-multiplier characterization of polynomial convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of global polynomial convexity through the midpoint-convexity polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}] is convex if and only if there exist nontrivial sum-of-squares polynomials p,q\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}] such that, for all \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\left(f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{y})-2f\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}{2}\right)\right)=q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is convex exactly when there are nontrivial sum-of-squares polynomials p and q such that multiplying its midpoint-convexity difference by p yields q identically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \exists\text{ nontrivial }p,q\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}]\ \forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\left(f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{y})-2f\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}{2}\right)\right)=q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Polynomial-Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex polynomial minimization over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be convex on \(C\). A convex polynomial-objective model is \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\] Every local minimizer is global, and the minimizer set is convex. If \(C\) is compact, the infimum is attained; more generally, attainment follows when \(C\) is closed and \(f\) is coercive on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex polynomial-objective model minimizes a convex polynomial on a convex set; local minima are global, with attainment under compactness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every local minimizer is global, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS-Convex Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial models whose objective and inequality-function Hessians admit sum-of-squares matrix factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is SOS-convex if there exists a polynomial matrix \(H(x)\) such that \[\nabla^2f(x)=H(x)^{\mathsf T}H(x).\] Under the inequality convention \(g_i(x)\le0\), an SOS-convex polynomial model minimizes an SOS-convex polynomial \(f_0\) subject to SOS-convex polynomial inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\). The Hessian factorization gives \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), so every SOS-convex polynomial is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS-convexity means that a polynomial Hessian has a polynomial matrix Gram factorization. SOS-convex objectives and less-than-or-equal constraint functions therefore define a convex polynomial model.
assumptions_latex: There exists a polynomial matrix \(H(x)\) satisfying \(\nabla^2f(x)=H(x)^{\mathsf T}H(x)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), hence \(f\) is convex.

notation.meaning: SOS-convex polynomial inequality function under the convention g_i less than or equal to zero

A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]\) is SOS-convex if there exist \(p\in\mathbb N\) and \(M\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]^{n\times p}\) such that

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials and truncated moment functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An algebraic Jensen inequality for normalized truncated sequences whose order-\(d\) moment matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]_{2d}\) be SOS-convex. If \(\mathbf y=(y_{\boldsymbol\alpha})_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb N_{2d}^n}\) satisfies \(y_{\mathbf0}=1\) and \(\mathbf M_d(\mathbf y)\succeq0\), then \[L_{\mathbf y}(f)\geq f\!\left(L_{\mathbf y}(\mathbf x)\right),\qquad L_{\mathbf y}(\mathbf x)=\left(L_{\mathbf y}(x_1),\ldots,L_{\mathbf y}(x_n)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized truncated moment functional with a positive semidefinite moment matrix satisfies Jensen's inequality for every SOS-convex polynomial of degree at most 2d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\mathbf y}(f)\geq f\!\left(L_{\mathbf y}(\mathbf x)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of SOS-convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes SOS-convexity through the Hessian, midpoint gap, and first-order remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real polynomial \(g\), the following are equivalent: (a) \(g\) is SOS-convex; (b) \(\nabla^2g(\mathbf{x})\) is an SOS matrix polynomial; (c) \(\frac12g(\mathbf{x})+\frac12g(\mathbf{y})-g\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}2\right)\) is SOS in \((\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\); and (d) \(g(\mathbf{x})-g(\mathbf{y})-\nabla g(\mathbf{y})^T(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\) is SOS in \((\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS-convexity is equivalent to an SOS Hessian, an SOS midpoint-convexity gap, and an SOS first-order convexity remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(a)}\iff\text{(b)}\iff\text{(c)}\iff\text{(d)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SDP lifts under SOS-convexity or strict quasiconcavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient curvature conditions for exact moment semidefinite representations of compact convex basic semialgebraic sets, subject to Assumption 2.14.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\geq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be convex and compact with nonempty interior, and suppose Assumption 2.14 holds. If for every \(j\), either \(-g_j\) is SOS-convex or \(g_j\) is strictly quasiconcave on \(K\), then there exists \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that \[K=\left\{z:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{s(2d)},\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ M_{d-v_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ \forall j,\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ \forall i\right\}.\] Hence \(K\) is semidefinite representable. If \(-g_j\) is SOS-convex for every \(j\), then for every \(d\geq\max_jv_j\), \[K=\left\{z:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{s(2d)},\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ L_y(g_j)\geq0\ \forall j,\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ \forall i\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Assumption 2.14, a compact convex basic semialgebraic set with nonempty interior has an exact moment SDP lift when every defining polynomial satisfies the stated SOS-convexity or strict-quasiconcavity condition. In the all-SOS-convex case, scalar moment inequalities replace localizing-matrix constraints.

\forall j,\ [-g_j\text{ is SOS-convex}]\lor[g_j\text{ is strictly quasiconcave on }K]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ has the stated exact moment-matrix SDP representation and hence is SDr}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact SOS relaxation and minimizer extraction for SOS-convex programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness at the source-defined relaxation order and first-moment minimizer extraction for a Slater-regular SOS-convex polynomial program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) satisfy Slater's condition, and let \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)>-\infty\). If \(f\) and every \(-g_j\) are SOS-convex, then, at the source-defined order \(d\), \(f^*=\rho_d=\rho_d^*\). Moreover, if \(y\) is an optimal solution of the moment relaxation, then \(x^*:=(L_y(x_1),\ldots,L_y(x_n))\in K\) and \(f(x^*)=f^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Semialgebraic-Set Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization on convex feasible sets described by finitely many polynomial inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex basic semialgebraic feasible set is a set \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,r\}\] that is convex, where all \(g_i\) and \(h_j\) are real polynomials. A sufficient representation condition is that every \(g_i\) is convex and every \(h_j\) is affine. A convex semialgebraic-set model minimizes a convex polynomial over such a nonempty set \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These models minimize a convex polynomial over a convex set described by polynomial inequalities and equalities; convex inequalities and affine equalities suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing a convex polynomial over \(K\) is a convex polynomial optimization model.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Optimization Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization models whose cross-block interaction is bilinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty feasible sets. A bilinear optimization model has objective \[\inf_{x\in X,\ y\in Y}\ x^{\mathsf T}Ay+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha,\] possibly together with constraints that are affine in \(x\) for each fixed \(y\) and affine in \(y\) for each fixed \(x\). The model is separately affine in its two variable blocks but is generally nonconvex jointly because of the products \(x_i y_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bilinear models are affine in either variable block when the other is fixed, but their cross-products generally destroy joint convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is affine in each block separately and generally nonconvex in \((x,y)\) jointly.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Box-Constrained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multilinear polynomial optimization over a Cartesian box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(\ell_i<u_i\). A multilinear box-constrained model has the form \[\min_{x\in B} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}c_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\] possibly with constraints \(g_j(x)\leq 0\), where every \(g_j\) has the same multilinear form. Equivalently, each participating polynomial is affine in every coordinate when all other coordinates are fixed. Because such a polynomial is coordinatewise affine, its unrestricted minimum and maximum over \(B\) are attained at vertices of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-constrained multilinear model optimizes polynomials that are affine in each coordinate separately; without additional constraints, extrema occur at box vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and any constraint polynomials are multilinear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the unconstrained model, \(\min_{x\in B}f(x)=\min_{x\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}f(x)\) and analogously for the maximum.

notation.meaning: coefficient of the square-free monomial indexed by S

knowledge_statements.title: Multiaffine Network Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorized multiaffine optimization on a network of variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite hypergraph and let each vertex \(v\) carry a block \(x_v\in B_v\subset\mathbb R^{n_v}\). A multiaffine network model is \[\min_{x\in\prod_{v\in V}B_v}\sum_{e\in E}\phi_e((x_v)_{v\in e})\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{e\in E}\psi_{je}((x_v)_{v\in e})\leq0,\] where every local factor \(\phi_e\) and \(\psi_{je}\) is affine in each incident block separately when the remaining blocks are fixed. The hypergraph records the interaction locality; it does not require joint affinity or convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Even-Degree Form Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of real homogeneous forms of even degree on normalized or compact sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=2k\) and let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a homogeneous form of degree \(d\), represented by a symmetric order-\(d\) tensor \(\mathcal A\) through \(p(x)=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes d}\rangle\). Even-degree form optimization seeks \[p_{\min}=\min_{x\in K}p(x)\quad\text{or}\quad p_{\max}=\max_{x\in K}p(x),\] where \(K\) is commonly the unit sphere or another compact basic semialgebraic set. Since \(p(-x)=p(x)\), antipodal points have equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even-degree form model optimizes a homogeneous polynomial on a normalized compact domain; its value is unchanged by reversing the sign of the variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both extrema exist, and \(p(-x)=p(x)\) whenever \(x,-x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Degree Form Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antipodal structure of odd-degree homogeneous optimization on centrally symmetric domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=2k+1\) and let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be homogeneous of degree \(d\). If \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and centrally symmetric, then \(p(-x)=-p(x)\) for every \(x\in K\). Consequently, \[\min_{x\in K}p(x)=-\max_{x\in K}p(x).\] In particular, optimizing an odd-degree form over the unit sphere reduces either extremum to the other, and every nonzero odd-degree form takes both positive and negative values there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a centrally symmetric compact set, an odd-degree form changes sign at antipodal points, so its minimum is the negative of its maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in K}p(x)=-\max_{x\in K}p(x)\).

notation.meaning: central symmetry of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Eigenvalue Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real Z-eigenvalue formulation for symmetric tensors and sphere-constrained forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\in\operatorname{Sym}^m(\mathbb R^n)\). A real Z-eigenpair is a scalar-vector pair \((\lambda,x)\) satisfying \[\mathcal A x^{m-1}=\lambda x,\qquad x^\mathsf T x=1.\] For the homogeneous form \(f(x)=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle\), every first-order stationary point of its restriction to the unit sphere yields such a pair, with \(\lambda=f(x)\). Conversely, every Z-eigenpair is stationary for the sphere-constrained form problem. Thus extremal Z-eigenvalues are obtained by minimizing or maximizing \(f\) on the unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Z-eigenpairs of a real symmetric tensor are exactly stationary points of its homogeneous form on the Euclidean unit sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a real symmetric tensor of order \(m\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A x^{m-1}=\lambda x\) holds exactly at sphere-stationary points, with \(\lambda=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Singular-Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilinear singular values for real rectangular tensors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_m}\) and define \(F(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=\langle\mathcal A,x^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x^{(m)}\rangle\). A singular tuple consists of unit vectors \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{n_k}\) and a scalar \(\sigma\) such that, for every \(k\), \[\mathcal A\times_{j\ne k}x^{(j)}=\sigma x^{(k)},\qquad \|x^{(k)}\|_2=1.\] These equations are the first-order stationarity conditions for optimizing \(F\) over the product of unit spheres, and \(\sigma=F(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\).

Every factor vector has Euclidean norm one.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Tensor Spectral Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric spectral norm and its diagonal homogeneous-form reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real symmetric order-\(m\) tensor \(\mathcal A\in\operatorname{Sym}^m(\mathbb R^n)\), define its multilinear spectral norm over independent unit vectors. The symmetric spectral regime satisfies \[\max_{\|x^{(1)}\|_2=\cdots=\|x^{(m)}\|_2=1}\left|\left\langle\mathcal A,x^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x^{(m)}\right\rangle\right|=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\left|\left\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\right\rangle\right|.\] Hence a best rank-one spectral approximation may be chosen symmetric, and spectral optimization reduces to a homogeneous polynomial problem on one sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric tensor, the spectral norm can be computed using one repeated unit vector rather than independent mode vectors.
assumptions_latex: All norms on factor vectors are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\mathcal A\|_\sigma=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}|\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Tensor Spectral Regimes

At any maximizing tuple, signs may be chosen so that the contraction is nonnegative, and the associated first-order equations are \(\mathcal A\times_{j\ne k}x^{(j)}=\|\mathcal A\|_\sigma x^{(k)}\) for every mode \(k\). Unlike the symmetric regime, the factors inhabit distinct mode spaces and need not coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Rank Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polyadic rank and rank-constrained tensor optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\inigotimes_{k=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_k}\), its canonical polyadic rank is \[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)=\min\left\{r:X=
\sum_{i=1}^r u_i^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_i^{(m)}\right\},\] with \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(0)=0\). A tensor rank model minimizes a loss \(F(X)\) subject to \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\leq r\), or penalizes the loss by \(\lambda\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\). For \(m=2\) this is matrix rank; for \(m\geq3\), the feasible geometry can be nonclosed and substantially more singular.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Rank Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tensor nuclear norm as a convex gauge surrogate for CP rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal U\) be the set of rank-one tensors \(u^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u^{(m)}\) with \(\|u^{(k)}\|_2=1\) for every \(k\). The tensor nuclear norm is the atomic gauge \[\|X\|_*=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r|\alpha_i|:X=\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha_iU_i,
\ U_i\in\mathcal U\right\}.\] It is convex and is dual to the tensor spectral norm: \[\|X\|_*=\max_{\|Y\|_\sigma\leq1}\langle X,Y\rangle.\] Replacing CP rank by \(\|X\|_*\) therefore gives a norm-based convex surrogate, though it need not preserve every rank minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tensor nuclear norm gauges normalized rank-one atoms, is dual to the spectral norm, and supplies a convex surrogate for CP rank.
assumptions_latex: The ambient tensor space is finite-dimensional and real.
Rank-one atoms have unit Euclidean norm in every mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|X\|_*\) is convex and satisfies \(\|X\|_*=\max_{\|Y\|_\sigma\leq1}\langle X,Y\rangle\).

notation.meaning: set of normalized rank-one tensor atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratified Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of tensor feasible regions by exact CP rank.

Then \[C_{\leq r}=\bigcup_{s=0}^r C_s,\qquad C_r=C_{\leq r}\setminus C_{\leq r-1}.\] These exact-rank pieces form the CP-rank stratification of \(C\). For tensors of order at least three, bounded-rank sets need not be closed, so limits of sequences in \(C_{\leq r}\) may have rank exceeding \(r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Encodings of Combinatorial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies when a polynomial formulation exactly represents a finite combinatorial optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite feasible family with cost \(c:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R\). An exact polynomial encoding consists of a basic semialgebraic set \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ h_k(x)=0\}\] and a decoding map \(\phi:K\to\mathcal C\) such that \(\phi\) is bijective and \(f(x)=c(\phi(x))\) for every \(x\in K\). Under these conditions, \[\min_{u\in\mathcal C}c(u)=\min_{x\in K}f(x),\] and minimizers correspond through \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact polynomial encoding bijectively represents combinatorial feasible objects and preserves their costs, hence preserves optimal values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{u\in\mathcal C}c(u)=\min_{x\in K}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Valued Polynomial Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Loewner order to define minimization of a symmetric polynomial-matrix objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be feasible and let \(F\in\mathbb S^r[x]\). A matrix-valued polynomial objective model seeks Loewner-minimal values of \(F(x)\) over \(K\). A feasible point \(x^\star\in K\) is Loewner-minimal if no \(y\in K\) satisfies both \(F(y)\preceq F(x^\star)\) and \(F(y)\ne F(x^\star)\). For any weight \(W\succeq0\), scalarization produces the polynomial objective \(x\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(WF(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a symmetric polynomial matrix, and solutions are minimal under the positive-semidefinite order; positive-semidefinite trace weights yield scalar polynomial objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is minimal}\iff\nexists y\in K:\ F(y)\preceq F(x^\star),\ F(y)\ne F(x^\star)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Loewner minimality is the canonical partial-order formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Loewner-minimality formulation and trace scalarization are mathematically plausible and the definition fits the terminal, but no inspectable citation is supplied. A source addressing matrix-valued optimization under the Loewner order is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Convex Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matrix convexity for symmetric polynomial-matrix mappings on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(F\in\mathbb S^r[x]\). The mapping \(F\) is matrix convex on \(C\) when, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preceq \theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y).\] A matrix-convex polynomial model minimizes \(F\) in the Loewner order, or a monotone scalarization of \(F\), over a convex feasible set; equivalently, every quadratic form \(x\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}F(x)v\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric polynomial matrix is matrix convex when it satisfies Jensen’s inequality in the Loewner order, equivalently after every quadratic-form scalarization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is matrix convex on }C\iff v^{\mathsf T}F(\cdot)v\text{ is convex on }C\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Degree Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records total and coordinatewise degrees of a scalar polynomial objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonzero objective polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), its objective degree profile is \[D_{\mathrm{obj}}(f):=(d;\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n),\qquad d:=\deg f,\quad \delta_i:=\deg_{x_i}f.\] Here \(d\) is the largest total exponent among monomials with nonzero coefficient, while \(\delta_i\) is the largest exponent of \(x_i\). Consequently, \(\max_i\delta_i\le d\le\sum_i\delta_i\). For the zero polynomial, every degree component is assigned \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective degree profile records a polynomial’s total degree and its degree in each decision variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{obj}}(f)=(\deg f;\deg_{x_1}f,\ldots,\deg_{x_n}f)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure and recognition of odd-degree quasiconvex and pseudoconvex polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ridge-polynomial characterization and fixed-degree polynomial-time recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}] have odd degree. It is quasiconvex only if and only if it has the form f(\mathbf{x})=h(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{x}) for some nonzero \mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n and a monotone univariate polynomial h; the same representation characterizes pseudoconvexity, with the additional requirement that h' have no real root. Moreover, for every fixed odd degree d, quasiconvexity and pseudoconvexity of degree-d polynomials can each be decided in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd-degree quasiconvex polynomial depends on a single linear form through a monotone univariate polynomial. Odd-degree pseudoconvex polynomials have the same ridge form, additionally with a derivative having no real zero. For every fixed odd degree, both properties can be recognized in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\mathbf{x})=h(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{x});\quad f\text{ pseudoconvex}\implies h'(t)\neq0\ \forall t\in\mathbb{R};\quad\text{for fixed odd }d,\text{ recognition is polynomial-time.}

children.title: Degree-Mismatch Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models with materially different objective and constraint degree scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Mismatch Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies constrained models by the gap between objective and maximum constraint degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a polynomial optimization problem with nonzero objective \(f\) and nonzero constraints \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\). Let \(d_0:=\deg f\) and \(d_c:=\max_j\deg g_j\). Its degree-mismatch index is \(\Delta:=d_0-d_c\). The model is objective-dominant when \(\Delta>0\), degree-balanced when \(\Delta=0\), and constraint-dominant when \(\Delta<0\). The magnitude \(|\Delta|\) records the total-degree gap but does not by itself determine convexity, boundedness, or computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the objective degree with the largest constraint degree: the model is objective-dominant, balanced, or constraint-dominant according to the sign of their difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=\deg f-\max_j\deg g_j\).

children.title: Even-Degree Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model classes dominated by even total degrees.

knowledge_statements.title: Even-Degree Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a sufficient boundedness condition for unconstrained even-degree polynomial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have even degree \(2r\ge2\), and let \(f_{2r}\) denote its leading homogeneous component. If \(f_{2r}(u)>0\) for every \(u\ne0\), then \(f\) is coercive: \[\|x\|\to\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)\to+\infty.\] Consequently, every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is compact, and \(f\) attains a finite global minimum on \(\mathbb R^n\). Even degree alone is insufficient without a condition on the leading form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even-degree polynomial with a positive-definite leading form is coercive and attains a global minimum; even degree by itself does not ensure boundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is coercive and }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Parity Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies models whose objective-constraint degree vector contains both degree parities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constrained polynomial model with nonzero objective \(f\) and nonzero constraints \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), define its degree-parity profile by \[P:=\bigl(\deg f\bmod 2,\deg g_1\bmod 2,\ldots,\deg g_m\bmod 2\bigr).\] The model lies in a mixed-parity regime exactly when \(P\) contains both \(0\) and \(1\); equivalently, at least one polynomial among \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) has even total degree and at least one has odd total degree.

children.title: Parity-Dependent Boundedness
children.top_down_role: Boundedness behavior associated with polynomial degree parity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Dependent Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained real-domain boundedness; even degree is necessary, while a positive-definite leading form is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=p_d+p_{d-1}+\cdots+p_0\), where each \(p_k\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\) and \(p_d\ne0\). If \(d\) is odd, then \(p\) is unbounded both above and below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Consequently, a nonconstant polynomial that is bounded above or bounded below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) must have even degree. Even degree alone does not imply boundedness. If \(p_d(v)>0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), then \(p\) is coercive, bounded below, and attains a finite global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant real polynomial bounded on either side must have even degree. Even degree alone is insufficient, while a positive-definite leading form guarantees coercivity and attainment of a finite global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(p_d\) is the degree-\(d\) homogeneous component of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p\) is bounded above or below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(d\) is even; if \(p_d(v)>0\) for every \(v\ne0\), then \(p\) is coercive and attains a finite global minimum.

notation.meaning: Leading homogeneous component of the polynomial.

children.title: Homogeneous Polynomial Structure
children.top_down_role: Models whose relevant polynomial components share ordinary scaling structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Polynomial Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary homogeneity of nonzero polynomials under uniform scalar dilation of all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0^n}c_\alpha x^\alpha\) be nonzero with finite support. The polynomial \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\) if every \(\alpha\) with \(c_\alpha\ne0\) satisfies \(|\alpha|=d\). Equivalently, \(p(tx)=t^d p(x)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For nonzero \(p\), the degree \(d\) is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero polynomial is homogeneous of degree d when all supported monomials have total degree d, equivalently when uniform scaling multiplies its value by the d-th power.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\) exactly when \(p(tx)=t^d p(x)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Ordinary total degree of a multi-index.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of an ordinary homogeneous polynomial

children.title: Quasihomogeneous Polynomial Structure
children.top_down_role: Models whose polynomial components follow weighted scaling structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is \(w\)-quasihomogeneous of weighted degree \(D\) exactly when \(p(t^{w_1}x_1,\ldots,t^{w_n}x_n)=t^D p(x)\) for all \(t>0\).

notation.meaning: Weighted degree of a monomial exponent.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted-homogeneity definition with positive rational weights
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-weight polynomial quasihomogeneity; weights may be cleared to positive integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\). The polynomial is quasihomogeneous with weight vector \(w\) and weighted degree \(D\) when every \(\alpha\) with \(c_\alpha\ne0\) satisfies \(w\cdot\alpha=D\). Equivalently, for the anisotropic dilation \(\delta_t(x)=(t^{w_1}x_1,\ldots,t^{w_n}x_n)\), one has \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t>0\). Multiplying \(w\) and \(D\) by a common positive number leaves the structure unchanged; rational weights can therefore be normalized to integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is quasihomogeneous when all its monomials share one positive weighted degree, equivalently when anisotropic coordinate scaling multiplies the polynomial by a fixed power.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted coordinate degree is \(\deg_w(x^\alpha)=w\cdot\alpha\), and \(\deg_w(p)=\max_{\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)}w\cdot\alpha\) for \(p\ne0\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted-degree grading of a polynomial ring

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate weights induce a grading or filtration on the polynomial ring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign coordinate \(x_i\) the positive weight \(w_i\). The weighted degree of the monomial \(x^\alpha\) is \(\deg_w(x^\alpha)=w\cdot\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\alpha_i\). For a nonzero polynomial \(p=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\), define \(\deg_w(p)=\max\{w\cdot\alpha:c_\alpha\ne0\}\). Its weighted-degree-\(D\) component is the sum of those terms satisfying \(w\cdot\alpha=D\). Consequently, multiplication adds weighted degrees, while addition satisfies \(\deg_w(p+q)\le\max\{\deg_w(p),\deg_w(q)\}\) whenever \(p+q\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive coordinate weights assign each monomial the dot product of its exponent and weight vectors; a polynomial's weighted degree is the largest such value in its support.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Degree Coordinate Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-degree definition and stated algebraic properties are standard and internally consistent, but the record has no source or locator.

children.title: Scaling-Orbit Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set and objective geometry associated with homogeneous scaling orbits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each orbit \(\mathcal{O}_w(x)=\{\delta_t(x):t>0\}\) satisfies \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\), so its intersection with \(\{p=0\}\) is either empty or the entire orbit.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct geometric consequence of weighted homogeneity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of positive anisotropic dilation orbits and invariant polynomial level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maps \(\delta_t\) form an action of \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) because \(\delta_s(\delta_t(x))=\delta_{st}(x)\). Quasihomogeneity gives \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\) along every orbit. Hence the zero set \(Z(p)=\{x:p(x)=0\}\) is a union of scaling orbits. If \(D>0\) and \(p(x)\ne0\), the sign of \(p\) is constant on \(\mathcal{O}_w(x)\), and each positive level \(p=c\) on that orbit is reached at most once. For uniform weights this reduces to ordinary radial rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted dilations partition space into scaling orbits. A quasihomogeneous polynomial scales by one power along each orbit, making its zero set orbit-invariant and preserving sign.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Orbit Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit action, scaling law, zero-set invariance, and sign claim are correct under the stated positive-weight assumptions, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Multidegree Structure
children.top_down_role: Polynomial classes indexed by degree profiles across individual variables or variable groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidegree Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise multidegree for a polynomial in fixed variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(d_i=\max\{\alpha_i:\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\}\). The coordinate multidegree is \(\operatorname{mdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\). Equivalently, \(d_i\) is the degree of \(p\) as a univariate polynomial in \(x_i\) over the polynomial ring in the remaining variables. Every \(\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\) satisfies \(\alpha_i\le d_i\) for every \(i\), but \((d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) need not belong to \(\operatorname{supp}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multidegree records the largest exponent attained in each coordinate separately; these maxima need not occur together in any single monomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate multidegree of \(p\) is \(\operatorname{mdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\), where \(d_i=\max_{c_\alpha\ne0}\alpha_i\).

notation.meaning: Degree of p in coordinate variable i.

children.title: Block-Degree Structure
children.top_down_role: Polynomial classes indexed by degree bounds within designated variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Degree Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total degree is measured separately within each fixed variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_m\), assign each exponent \(\alpha\) the block-degree vector \((|\alpha|_{B_1},\ldots,|\alpha|_{B_m})\), where \(|\alpha|_{B_j}=\sum_{i\in B_j}\alpha_i\). For nonzero \(p\), define \(\operatorname{bdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\), where \(d_j=\max_{\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)}|\alpha|_{B_j}\). Every supported monomial lies in \(\prod_{j=1}^m\{0,\ldots,d_j\}\), but the maximal corner need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After variables are partitioned into blocks, block degree records the largest total exponent appearing within each block, with maxima computed independently.
assumptions_latex: The variables are partitioned into nonempty disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block-degree vector is \(\operatorname{bdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\), where \(d_j=\max_{c_\alpha\ne0}\sum_{i\in B_j}\alpha_i\).

Total exponent contributed by block j.

children.title: Cross-Block Degree Coupling
children.top_down_role: Degree patterns created by monomials spanning multiple variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Degree Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based coupling among degree choices of distinct variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\alpha\in A\), define \(\gamma(\alpha)=(|\alpha|_{B_1},\ldots,|\alpha|_{B_m})\) and \(\Gamma(A)=\{\gamma(\alpha):\alpha\in A\}\). Let \(\Gamma_j(A)\) be the projection of \(\Gamma(A)\) onto coordinate \(j\). The support has no cross-block degree coupling when \(\Gamma(A)=\Gamma_1(A)\times\cdots\times\Gamma_m(A)\), and it has cross-block degree coupling when this equality fails. This predicate concerns jointly realized degree patterns, not coefficient factorization or functional separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block degrees are coupled when some combination of degrees observed separately in different blocks never occurs jointly in the polynomial's monomial support.
assumptions_latex: The variables are partitioned into nonempty disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-block degree coupling is present exactly when \(\Gamma(A)\ne\Gamma_1(A)\times\cdots\times\Gamma_m(A)\).

notation.meaning: Set of jointly realized block-degree vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex circuits with one relative-interior exponent, as used in sparse polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simplex circuit support is a set \(A=\{\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r),\beta\}\) such that \(\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)\) are affinely independent and \(\beta\) lies in the relative interior of their convex hull. Equivalently, unique coefficients \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_r>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j=1\) and \(\beta=\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j\alpha(j)\). The set \(A\) is minimally affinely dependent and hence is a circuit of the affine exponent configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex circuit consists of affinely independent outer exponents and one exponent in their relative interior, yielding a unique strictly positive barycentric relation.

children.title: Simplex Supports

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex supports whose Newton polytope is a simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponent set \(A=\{\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)\}\) is a simplex support when its points are affinely independent, equivalently when \(\alpha(1)-\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)-\alpha(0)\) are linearly independent. Its convex hull \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is then an \(r\)-dimensional simplex. Every \(y\in\Delta\) has a unique representation \(y=\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j\alpha(j)\), where \(\lambda_j\ge0\) for every \(j\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j=1\). If a polynomial has support exactly \(A\), then its Newton polytope is \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex support is an affinely independent exponent set. Its convex hull is a simplex, and every point in that hull has unique barycentric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is a simplex support exactly when its elements are affinely independent; then \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is an \(r\)-simplex.
