knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H\le S_n\), the problem \(\inf\{f(x):g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,s\}\) has permutation symmetry \(H\) if, for every \(\pi\in H\), \(f(\pi x)=f(x)\) and \(g_j(\pi x)=g_j(x)\) for every \(j\) and every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Consequently, its feasible set and objective values are constant on every \(H\)-orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model has permutation symmetry when a specified group of coordinate permutations leaves every constraint polynomial and the objective unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The presentation-level definition is mathematically coherent and fits Permutation Symmetry, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Sign-Flip Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model invariance under selected variable sign changes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is invariant under the sign flip \(s_J\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous invariance of all model polynomials under one coordinate sign flip.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial optimization model has sign-flip symmetry on \(J\) if \(p(s_Jx)=p(x)\) for every \(p\in\{f,g_1,\ldots,g_s\}\) and every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For an individual polynomial \(p(x)=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha x^\alpha\), this is equivalent to \(\sum_{i\in J}\alpha_i\equiv0\pmod 2\) for every \(\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign-flip symmetry negates selected coordinates without changing any model polynomial; equivalently, every active monomial has even total exponent on those coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Flip Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and exponent-parity equivalence are precise and appropriate, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Exponent-Parity Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Support patterns organized by parity classes of monomial exponents.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_p\) is the exponent-parity structure of \(p\).

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise reduction of an exponent vector modulo two.
Set of parity vectors of active monomials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity data of active exponent vectors, viewed over \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponent-parity structure of \(p\) is \(P_p=\{\alpha\bmod2:p_\alpha\ne0\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n\). If \(u\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\) encodes the sign change \(x_i\mapsto(-1)^{u_i}x_i\), then the monomial \(x^\alpha\) is multiplied by \((-1)^{u^\mathsf{T}\bar\alpha}\). Hence \(p\) is invariant under this sign change exactly when \(u^\mathsf{T}v=0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_2\) for every \(v\in P_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent parity reduces each active monomial's exponent vector modulo two and thereby determines exactly which coordinate sign changes preserve the polynomial.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponent-Parity Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity-support representation correctly captures sign invariance and fits the leaf, but it lacks a source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Sign–Parity Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model classes where sign actions align with exponent-parity structure.

assumptions_latex: \(p_1,\ldots,p_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) are the objective and constraint polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model's sign-parity interaction regime is determined by \(L^\perp\), where \(L=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(P)\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal complement over the binary field.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary orthogonality links exponent patterns to the model's sign-symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode a coordinate sign change by \(u\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\), acting as \(x_i\mapsto(-1)^{u_i}x_i\). The change preserves every \(p_k\) if and only if \(u^\mathsf{T}v=0\) for every \(v\in P\). Therefore the admissible sign changes are exactly \(L^\perp\). The regimes range from full sign symmetry when \(L=\{0\}\), through intermediate symmetry when \(0<\dim L<n\), to no nontrivial sign symmetry when \(L=\mathbb{F}_2^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The span of all active exponent parities and its binary orthogonal complement classify full, partial, and trivial model-level sign symmetry.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign–Parity Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary orthogonality duality is internally consistent and correctly distinguishes full, intermediate, and trivial sign symmetry, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Broken Sign Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Perturbations or terms that destroy an otherwise present sign invariance.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proposed sign symmetry is broken by the model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the precise monomial obstruction to a proposed coordinate sign symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sign symmetry encoded by \(u\) is broken if and only if some model polynomial \(p_k\) contains an active monomial \((p_k)_\alpha x^\alpha\) with \(u^\mathsf{T}\bar\alpha=1\) in \(\mathbb{F}_2\). Under the associated coordinate sign change, that monomial changes sign. Since distinct monomials are linearly independent, \(p_k\) is not invariant, and consequently the full polynomial optimization model lacks the proposed symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed sign symmetry is broken exactly when some active monomial has odd parity against the sign-flip pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Broken Sign Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monomial obstruction is a correct failure-boundary formulation, but the record lacks an inspectable supporting source.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts linearly on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polynomial optimization model is \(G\)-invariant.

notation.meaning: Linear action of group element g on x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear-group invariance of the objective and a fixed constraint presentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\inf\{f(x):x\in K\}\) is a group-invariant polynomial model under \(G\) if \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) and \(g_j(g\cdot x)=g_j(x)\) for every \(g\in G\), every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and every \(j\). These identities imply \(g\cdot K=K\), and the objective is constant on each orbit \(G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial model is group-invariant when a linear group action preserves every displayed constraint polynomial and the objective, hence preserves feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Invariant Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly describes invariance of a fixed polynomial constraint presentation and implies orbitwise constancy, but no source or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compact real algebraic variety is a set \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_i(x)=0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}\) that is compact in the Euclidean topology. Since every polynomial zero set is closed, compactness is equivalent to boundedness. If \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)\ne\varnothing\), each polynomial \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) attains both \(\min_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\) and \(\max_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact real algebraic variety is a bounded common real zero set of finitely many polynomials; polynomial objectives attain their extrema on every nonempty such set.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Algebraic Varieties

children.title: Compact Smooth Manifolds

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Smooth Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact polynomial equality loci for which zero is a regular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_1(x)=\cdots=h_r(x)=0\}\). If \(M\) is nonempty and compact and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=r\) for every \(x\in M\), then \(0\in\mathbb{R}^r\) is a regular value of \(h\), so \(M\) is a compact smooth embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of dimension \(n-r\). At every \(x\in M\), its tangent space is \(T_xM=\ker Dh(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty compact polynomial equality locus is a compact smooth embedded manifold of dimension n minus r when the defining Jacobian has full row rank r at every point of the locus; its tangent space is the Jacobian kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a compact smooth embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of dimension \(n-r\), with \(T_xM=\ker Dh(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of h at x.
Tangent space at x under the regular-value hypothesis.

children.title: Singular Compact Varieties
children.top_down_role: Compact algebraic feasible sets containing singular loci.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Compact Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-dimensional compact real algebraic varieties having at least one Jacobian-singular point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\in\mathbb R[x]^m\) and \(V=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h(x)=0\}\). Assume that \(V\) is nonempty, compact, and pure-dimensional of dimension \(d\). The variety \(V\) is singular when its singular locus \[\operatorname{Sing}(V)=\{x\in V:\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)<n-d\}\] is nonempty. A polynomial optimization problem \(\inf_{x\in V}f(x)\), with \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\), is then a singular compact-variety model; compactness guarantees attainment despite the singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact pure-dimensional algebraic feasible set is singular if its defining Jacobian loses the expected rank somewhere; every polynomial objective still attains its minimum on it.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is nonempty, compact, and pure-dimensional of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sing}(V)\ne\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in V}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of the defining polynomial map
real dimension of the pure-dimensional variety
Jacobian singular locus of the variety

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold-Constrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained polynomial optimization on a compact smooth real algebraic manifold defined by a regular polynomial level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\leq n\), let \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be polynomial, and set \(M=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h(x)=0\}\). A manifold-constrained polynomial model is \[f^*=\min_{x\in M}f(x),\qquad f\in\mathbb R[x],\] where \(M\) is nonempty and compact and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=m\) for every \(x\in M\). Then \(M\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(d=n-m\), and the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes a polynomial over a nonempty compact polynomial equality set at which the equality Jacobian has full row rank; the feasible set is a smooth manifold of dimension n-m and the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(n-m\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in M}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of the polynomial equality map

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Noncompact Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment for polynomial objectives coercive relative to a closed noncompact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and noncompact, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The objective is coercive on \(K\) when \[\lim_{\substack{x\in K\\ \|x\|\to\infty}}f(x)=+\infty.\] Every sublevel set \(\{x\in K:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is then compact. Consequently, \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\) is finite and is attained by at least one point of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed noncompact feasible set, a polynomial growing to positive infinity along every escaping feasible sequence has compact sublevels and attains a finite minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*>-\infty\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: global infimum of the objective over the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Noncoercive Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact polynomial models whose minimum exists without relative coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and noncompact, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The model is attained but noncoercive when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R,\qquad \{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}\ne\varnothing,\] while there exists a sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) such that \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(f(x_k)\not\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polynomial has a finite global minimizer on a closed noncompact feasible set, although some feasible sequence escapes to infinity without the objective tending to positive infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\), but \(f\) is not coercive on \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment at Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite infimum approached only by feasible sequences escaping every bounded region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). Nonattainment at infinity occurs when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R,\qquad \{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}=\varnothing.\] Every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) satisfying \(f(x_k)\to f^*\) then satisfies \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum is finite but no feasible point realizes it; because the feasible set is closed, every minimizing sequence must escape to infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty basic semialgebraic set and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The minimization model is unbounded below when \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty.\] Equivalently, for every \(M\in\mathbb R\) there exists \(x_M\in K\) such that \(f(x_M)<M\). Thus the model has neither a finite optimal value nor a global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Optimal Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial models whose finite infimum is realized by a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The optimal value is attained when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad \exists x^*\in K\;\; f(x^*)=f^*.\] Equivalently, the global solution set \(K^*=\{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}\) is nonempty. Attainment is distinct from merely having a finite infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal value is attained when the finite infimum equals the objective value at at least one feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moment formula for the best polynomial approximation of an optimizer coordinate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The optimizer mapping is considered under the unexpanded hypotheses referenced by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 14.5. Let \(g_k\in L_2(\varphi)\) be the \(k\)-th coordinate of the global-minimizer mapping, let \(M_d(\varphi)\) be the order-\(d\) moment matrix, and define \(u^d_\beta=\int_{\mathbf Y}\mathbf y^\beta g_k(\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\) for \(\beta\in\mathbb N_d^p\). If \(M_d(\varphi)\) is invertible and the degree-\(d\) polynomial \(p_d^*\) has coefficient vector \(\mathbf p_d^*=M_d(\varphi)^{-1}\mathbf u^d\), then \(p_d^*\) is a best degree-\(d\) approximation to \(g_k\) in \(L_2(\varphi)\). In the orthonormal-polynomial basis associated with \(\varphi\), its coefficients are the corresponding generalized moments \(\mathbf u^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best degree-d least-squares polynomial approximation of an optimizer-map coordinate is obtained by solving the moment-matrix normal equations. In the associated orthonormal polynomial basis, the approximation coefficients are the generalized moments of that coordinate.
assumptions_latex: u^d_\beta=\int_{\mathbf Y}\mathbf y^\beta g_k(\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\quad(\beta\in\mathbb N_d^p).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf p_d^*=M_d(\varphi)^{-1}\mathbf u^d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\int_{\mathbf Y}(p_d^*-g_k)^2\,d\varphi=\inf_{p\in\mathbb R[\mathbf y]_d}\int_{\mathbf Y}(p-g_k)^2\,d\varphi;\quad\text{in the associated orthonormal basis, the coefficients are }\mathbf u^d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of binary optimizer-coordinate probabilities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result is conditional on the unexpanded convergence hypotheses referenced by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses guaranteeing the parametric moment--SDP convergence used in Theorem 14.5, and let \((\mathbf z^d)\) be nearly optimal solutions of relaxations (14.14). For fixed \(k\in I\), if every optimal solution satisfies \(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1\) (respectively, \(0\)) for \(\varphi\)-almost every \(\mathbf y\in\mathbf Y\), then \(\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}=1\) (respectively, \(0\)). If, additionally, the optimal solution \(\mathbf x^*(\mathbf y)\) is unique for \(\varphi\)-almost every \(\mathbf y\), then \(\operatorname{Prob}_{\mathbf y\sim\varphi}(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1)=\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}\). Consequently, \(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1\) (respectively, \(0\)) almost everywhere if and only if this limit equals \(1\) (respectively, \(0\)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the assumed moment–SDP convergence conditions, an optimizer coordinate that is always 1 or always 0 almost everywhere forces the corresponding limiting relaxation moment to equal that value. When the optimizer is almost everywhere unique, the limiting moment equals the probability that the coordinate is 1, yielding an if-and-only-if criterion for an almost-surely fixed binary coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \text{The parametric moment--SDP convergence hypotheses referenced in Theorem 14.5 hold.}
\mathbf z^d\text{ is nearly optimal for relaxation (14.14) for each }d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[x_k^*(\mathbf y)=b\ \varphi\text{-a.e. for every optimizer}\bigr]\Rightarrow\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}=b\quad(b\in\{0,1\});\quad\text{under a.e. uniqueness, }\operatorname{Prob}(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1)=\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0},\text{ and the implication becomes an equivalence for }b\in\{0,1\}.

children.title: Nonattained Finite Infima
children.top_down_role: Model regimes with finite limiting values absent a feasible optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Finite Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial models with a finite infimum but an empty global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The model has a nonattained finite infimum when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) with \(f(x_\varepsilon)<f^*+\varepsilon\), but no feasible point has objective value \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is bounded below and can approach a finite infimum arbitrarily closely, but no feasible point realizes that value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)=\varnothing\).

children.title: Unbounded Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasible models whose objective values escape every finite bound in the optimizing direction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization regime characterized by arbitrarily low feasible objective values.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 General Minimization Problem p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial minimization problem is in an unbounded-objective regime precisely when, for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\), there exists \(x_M\in K\) such that \(f(x_M)<M\). Equivalently, there is a sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq K\) satisfying \(f(x_k)\to-\infty\). Thus the problem has no finite optimal value and no global minimizer with real objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization problem is objective-unbounded when feasible points attain arbitrarily negative objective values, equivalently when its infimum is negative infinity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is specified entirely by finitely many polynomials in \(\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a real polynomial optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization models over real affine coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real polynomial coordinate model is an optimization problem of the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq0\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad h_j(x)=0\ \ (j=1,\ldots,r),\] where \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m,h_1,\ldots,h_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Its feasible set is the basic closed semialgebraic set \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real polynomial coordinate model optimizes a real polynomial over real coordinates subject to finitely many real polynomial inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Real Polynomial Coordinate Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard and fits the container, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Complex Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model families expressed directly in complex coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All model functions belong to \(\mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard holomorphic polynomial coordinate model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Holomorphic polynomial models; real-valued Hermitian models are treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complex polynomial model is a finite system \[p_i(z)=0\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad q_j(z)\neq0\ \ (j=1,\ldots,r),\] or an optimization model built from such functions, where \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\) and every \(p_i,q_j\) lies in \(\mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\). Dependence is polynomial in \(z\) alone; conjugate variables \(\bar z\) do not occur. An order-valued objective requires an explicitly real-valued scalarization because \(\mathbb{C}\) has no compatible total order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complex polynomial model uses holomorphic polynomials in complex coordinates; optimization requires a separately specified real-valued objective or scalarization.
knowledge_statements.title: Complex Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The holomorphic model distinction is plausible, but the inclusion of inequations and real-valued scalarization conventions requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Hermitian Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Complex polynomial models organized by Hermitian coefficient or variable structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective and ordered constraints are real-valued polynomials in \((z,\bar z)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coefficient characterization of real-valued Hermitian polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued mixed polynomials on complex coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hermitian polynomial is a finite expression \[p(z,\bar z)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha\beta}z^\alpha\bar z^\beta\] whose coefficients satisfy \(c_{\alpha\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta\alpha}}\). Consequently \(p(z,\bar z)=\overline{p(z,\bar z)}\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\). A Hermitian polynomial optimization model minimizes such an objective subject to inequalities and equalities defined by Hermitian polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hermitian polynomial model uses mixed polynomials in complex variables and their conjugates whose coefficient symmetry makes every ordered model function real-valued.
knowledge_statements.title: Hermitian Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hermitian coefficient condition and real-valuedness claim are standard and appropriately classified as a definition, but no inspectable citation is provided.

children.title: Realification of Complex Models
children.top_down_role: Real-coordinate representations corresponding to complex polynomial models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complex feasibility and objective values are preserved under the bijection \(z\leftrightarrow(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: real and imaginary parts of a polynomial

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: substitution of real and imaginary coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion from complex coordinates to twice as many real coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in\mathbb{C}[z,\bar z]\), substitution of \(z=x+\mathrm{i}y\) and \(\bar z=x-\mathrm{i}y\) gives unique \(p_{\mathrm R},p_{\mathrm I}\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]\) such that \[p(z,\bar z)=p_{\mathrm R}(x,y)+\mathrm{i}p_{\mathrm I}(x,y).\] Hence \(p=0\) is equivalent to \(p_{\mathrm R}=p_{\mathrm I}=0\). If \(p\) is Hermitian, then \(p_{\mathrm I}=0\), and its value and every real polynomial inequality are preserved by \(z\leftrightarrow(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Writing each complex coordinate as real plus imaginary parts converts the model exactly into a real polynomial model in twice as many variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Realification of Complex Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The realification representation is mathematically standard and fits the exact container, but its equivalence and preservation claims lack a cited authoritative locator.

children.title: Conjugate-Symmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model classes distinguished by conjugation invariance or paired complex terms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(z,\bar z)=\overline{p(z,\bar z)}\) for all \(z\) exactly when \(c_{\alpha\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta\alpha}}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monomial coefficient comparison under conjugation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-level regimes under conjugation and variable exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the conjugate-exchange involution by \[p^*(z,\bar z)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\alpha\beta}}z^\beta\bar z^\alpha.\] The conjugate-symmetric regime is \(p=p^*\), equivalently \(c_{\alpha\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta\alpha}}\) for all \(\alpha,\beta\); then \(p\) is real-valued. The conjugate-skew regime is \(p=-p^*\); then \(p\) is purely imaginary-valued. Every mixed polynomial decomposes uniquely as \(p=(p+p^*)/2+(p-p^*)/2\) into these two regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugate symmetry is the coefficient condition obtained by conjugating coefficients and exchanging holomorphic and antiholomorphic exponents; it characterizes real-valued mixed polynomials.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Symmetry Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient characterization and symmetric/skew decomposition are plausible, but the involution convention and resulting value claims require authoritative sourcing.

children.title: Homogeneous Coordinate Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial models expressed using homogeneous coordinate systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each model polynomial satisfies \(F(\lambda X)=\lambda^dF(X)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a homogeneous polynomial system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial systems expressed in homogeneous coordinates before quotienting by scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homogeneous coordinate model is a finite polynomial system in \(X_0,\ldots,X_n\) in which each polynomial \(F\) is homogeneous of some degree \(d\), meaning \[F(\lambda X)=\lambda^dF(X)\] for every scalar \(\lambda\). Its zero constraints are invariant under every nonzero rescaling \(X\mapsto\lambda X\). Inequalities are scale-invariant only after fixing an admissible normalization or imposing an even-degree sign-compatible convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous coordinate model uses polynomials whose monomials have a common degree, making zero constraints invariant under nonzero coordinate scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Coordinate Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the container, but the conclusion uses one common degree d whereas the statement permits each polynomial to have its own degree. An authoritative source is also absent.

children.title: Projective Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model families interpreted on real or complex projective spaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is well-defined on equivalence classes \([X]\in\mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{F})\).

notation.meaning: projective class of a nonzero vector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard homogeneous-coordinate definition of a projective algebraic model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-invariant polynomial models on real or complex projective space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projective polynomial model has variable \([X]\in\mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{F})\), where \(X\in\mathbb{F}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(X\sim\lambda X\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{F}^{\times}\). Homogeneous equations \[F_i(X)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)\] define a feasible subset independent of the representative because \(F_i(\lambda X)=\lambda^{d_i}F_i(X)\). An objective on projective space must likewise be scale-invariant, for example a ratio of equally homogeneous quantities wherever its denominator is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projective polynomial model treats nonzero homogeneous coordinate vectors differing by scale as the same point and uses scale-invariant constraints and objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projective model definition and scale-invariance requirements fit the container, but no source with a specific locator supports the formulation.

children.title: Points at Infinity
children.top_down_role: Projective boundary structure relevant to polynomial feasible sets or objectives.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Points at infinity of the projective closure satisfy \(X_0=0\) and the leading homogeneous equations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of an affine model inside its projective closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an affine polynomial system, homogenize every equation and take its projective zero set. A point at infinity is a projective feasible point \([X_0:X_1:\cdots:X_n]\) with \(X_0=0\). If \(f=\sum_{k=0}^df_k\), where \(f_k\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\), then \[f^{\mathrm h}(0,X)=f_d(X).\] Thus candidate directions at infinity are nonzero vectors \(X\) satisfying the relevant leading homogeneous equations, subject to any additional equations required by the projective closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points at infinity are projective closure points with homogenizing coordinate zero; leading homogeneous terms determine their candidate directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Points at Infinity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No authoritative citation is supplied. Moreover, homogenizing a chosen generating system may introduce extraneous components at infinity unless the projective closure or saturation convention is specified precisely.

children.title: Affine–Projective Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Model-level correspondence between affine polynomial data and projective representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\mathrm h}(1,x)=f(x)\), and homogeneous \(F\) is recovered from its chart polynomial on \(X_0\neq0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard homogenization and dehomogenization identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard correspondence between affine space and the chart \(X_0\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The embedding \(x\mapsto[1:x_1:\cdots:x_n]\) identifies \(\mathbb{F}^n\) with the projective chart \(U_0\). For \(f\) of degree at most \(d\), define \[f^{\mathrm h}(X_0,X)=X_0^df(X/X_0).\] Then \(f^{\mathrm h}\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\) and \(f^{\mathrm h}(1,x)=f(x)\). Conversely, a homogeneous polynomial \(F\) of degree \(d\) restricts to \(f(x)=F(1,x)\), and on \(X_0\neq0\), \(F(X_0,X)=X_0^df(X/X_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization embeds an affine polynomial model into projective space, while setting the homogenizing coordinate to one recovers the affine model on its standard chart.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine–Projective Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogenization and dehomogenization identities are standard and the representation kind fits, but the record has no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Affine-Chart Models
children.top_down_role: Projective polynomial models represented within selected affine charts.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chart \(U_k\) is coordinatized bijectively by \(\mathbb{F}^n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard affine charts of projective space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate representation of a projective model on one nonvanishing-coordinate chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(k\), every projective point in \(U_k\) has a unique representative with \(X_k=1\). Its affine coordinates are \(u_i=X_i/X_k\) for \(i\neq k\), giving a bijection \(U_k\cong\mathbb{F}^n\). A homogeneous equation \(F(X)=0\) of degree \(d\) becomes the affine polynomial equation \[F(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1},1,u_{k+1},\ldots,u_n)=0.\] The resulting chart model represents exactly the projective feasible points lying in \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a nonzero homogeneous coordinate and normalizing it to one gives an affine polynomial model for exactly that projective chart.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Chart Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chart representation is standard, but the field F used throughout the statement and notation is not introduced in the assumptions, and no authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Dehomogenized Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Affine polynomial models obtained from homogeneous coordinate representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dehomogenized model is equivalent to the homogeneous model restricted to \(X_k\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial model obtained by fixing one homogeneous coordinate to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dehomogenization of a homogeneous polynomial \(F\) in chart \(U_k\) is \[D_kF(u)=F(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1},1,u_{k+1},\ldots,u_n).\] If \(F\) has degree \(d\), then for every \(X\) with \(X_k\neq0\), \[F(X)=X_k^dD_kF\bigl((X_i/X_k)_{i\neq k}\bigr).\] Therefore homogeneous zero constraints and their dehomogenized polynomial constraints correspond exactly within \(U_k\); points with \(X_k=0\) are omitted and require another chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dehomogenization sets one nonzero homogeneous coordinate to one, producing polynomial constraints equivalent to the original homogeneous constraints within that chart.
knowledge_statements.title: Dehomogenized Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chartwise dehomogenization identity is standard and correctly classified as a representation, but the base field is not specified and no authoritative source locator is provided.

children.title: Chart Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation choices associated with different nonvanishing projective coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A chart family is valid for \(S\) exactly when \(S\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\).

notation.meaning: The affine chart where the i-th homogeneous coordinate is nonzero.
Dehomogenization of F in chart i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite affine-chart coverage for real projective polynomial models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I\subseteq\{0,ldots,n\}\), select the charts \(\{U_i:i\in I\}\). In chart \(U_i\), normalize \(X_i=1\) and replace each homogeneous polynomial \(F\) by its dehomogenization \(f_i\). The regime is complete for optimization over \(S\) if and only if \(S\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\). A single-chart regime at \(i\) is therefore valid exactly when \(S\cap\{[X]:X_i=0\}=\varnothing\); otherwise every omitted point belongs to an exceptional set and requires another chart or separate treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected affine charts represent the whole projective feasible set exactly when they cover it; one chart suffices only if no feasible point lies on its excluded coordinate hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.title: Chart Selection Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the chart-selection leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no source supports the projective coverage and optimization-equivalence claims. The statement also has a corrupted \ldots command. A sourced, repaired record is required.

children.title: Exceptional Sets under Dehomogenization
children.top_down_role: Projective loci omitted or altered by a selected dehomogenization.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{R})\) is defined by homogeneous polynomial constraints.
Dehomogenization is performed in the chart \(U_i=\{[X]:X_i\neq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exceptional set is \(E_i=S\cap\{[X]:X_i=0\}\), and chart equivalence holds precisely on \(S\setminus E_i\).

notation.meaning: Points of S excluded by the i-th affine chart.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of feasible points at the hyperplane excluded by an affine chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalization \(X_i=1\) is defined only on \(U_i\). Hence its exceptional set relative to \(S\) is \(E_i=S\cap\{[X]:X_i=0\}\). Dehomogenization induces a bijection between \(S\setminus E_i\) and the corresponding affine feasible set, but represents no point of \(E_i\). Consequently, optimization values and attainment are preserved by this single chart only when \(E_i=\varnothing\), or when an independent argument proves that deleting \(E_i\) cannot change the relevant infimum, supremum, or minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dehomogenization in one chart omits exactly the feasible points on its excluded coordinate hyperplane, so global optimization equivalence can fail there.
knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional Sets under Dehomogenization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and exceptional-set formula fit the leaf, but the claims about bijection and preservation of optimization values, attainment, and minimizers have no cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Polynomial Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polynomial reformulations obtained by adding finitely many variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An auxiliary-variable polynomial lifting of an optimization model over \(K\) is a polynomially described set \(\widehat K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) together with the projection \(\pi_x\). It is feasible-set exact when \(\pi_x(\widehat K)=K\). For an objective \(f:K\to\mathbb{R}\), a polynomial lifted objective \(F:\widehat K\to\mathbb{R}\) is optimization-exact for minimization when \(\inf\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in\widehat K\}=f(x)\) for every \(x\in K\). The stronger condition \(F(x,y)=f(x)\) for every \((x,y)\in\widehat K\) also implies optimization exactness. Consequently, minimizing \(F\) over \(\widehat K\) has the same infimum as minimizing \(f\) over \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial lifting adds variables and polynomial constraints whose projection recovers the original feasible set; minimization is exact when the infimum of the lifted objective on each feasible fiber equals the original objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_j(x)\geq0\ (j=1,\ldots,p),\ h_k(x)=0\ (k=1,\ldots,q)\}\) is a basic semialgebraic set.
\(P(x,y)\) is a finite system of polynomial equalities and inequalities defining \(\widehat K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifting is exact for minimization when \(\pi_x(\widehat K)=K\) and \(\inf\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in\widehat K\}=f(x)\) for every \(x\in K\).

notation.meaning: Lifted feasible set with auxiliary variables.

children.title: Epigraph Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted model interfaces based on upper objective or function bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar epigraph lifting for minimization over a prescribed nonempty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph representation of \(f\) on \(K\) is \(\operatorname{epi}_K(f)=\{(x,t)\in K\times\mathbb{R}:t-f(x)\geq0\}\). For each \(x\in K\), the least feasible \(t\) equals \(f(x)\). Therefore \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}_K(f)\}\). If the original infimum is attained, a pair \((x^*,t^*)\) solves the lifted problem exactly when \(x^*\) minimizes \(f\) on \(K\) and \(t^*=f(x^*)\). When \(f\) is polynomial and \(K\) has a polynomial description, this is a polynomial lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a function equals minimizing a scalar upper bound constrained to lie above its graph; at every attained lifted optimum, the bound equals the function value.
assumptions_latex: The lifted optimization problem minimizes the added scalar variable \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}_K(f)\}\).

notation.meaning: Epigraph of f relative to K.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: Hypograph Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted model interfaces based on lower objective or function bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar hypograph lifting for maximization over a prescribed nonempty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hypograph representation of \(f\) on \(K\) is \(\operatorname{hypo}_K(f)=\{(x,t)\in K\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)-t\geq0\}\). For each \(x\in K\), the greatest feasible \(t\) equals \(f(x)\). Therefore \(\sup_{x\in K}f(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}_K(f)\}\). If the original supremum is attained, a pair \((x^*,t^*)\) solves the lifted problem exactly when \(x^*\) maximizes \(f\) on \(K\) and \(t^*=f(x^*)\). When \(f\) is polynomial and \(K\) has a polynomial description, this is a polynomial lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing a function equals maximizing a scalar lower bound constrained to lie below its graph; at every attained lifted optimum, the bound equals the function value.
assumptions_latex: The lifted optimization problem maximizes the added scalar variable \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in K}f(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}_K(f)\}\).

notation.meaning: Hypograph of f relative to K.

children.title: Two-Sided Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted interfaces combining upper and lower graph restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Graph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph encoding by simultaneous upper and lower inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The two-sided graph representation imposes both \(t\geq f(x)\) and \(t\leq f(x)\). Thus \(\operatorname{gra}_K(f)=\operatorname{epi}_K(f)\cap\operatorname{hypo}_K(f)=\{(x,t)\in K\times\mathbb{R}:t=f(x)\}\). Equivalently, it is represented by the equality \(t-f(x)=0\). If \(K\) is basic semialgebraic and \(f\) is polynomial, the graph is basic semialgebraic and may be described by the constraints for \(K\) together with \(t-f(x)\geq0\) and \(f(x)-t\geq0\), or by the equivalent polynomial equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Imposing both epigraph and hypograph inequalities forces the auxiliary scalar to equal the function value, producing the exact graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gra}_K(f)=\operatorname{epi}_K(f)\cap\operatorname{hypo}_K(f)=\{(x,t):x\in K,\ t=f(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Epigraph and hypograph relative to K.

children.title: Exactness Boundaries for Graph Liftings
children.top_down_role: Model regimes where a lifted graph representation may admit extra projected points.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Boundaries for Graph Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction-dependent value exactness and failure of one-sided constraints to encode a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(K\), the epigraph lift \(t\geq f(x)\) is value-exact when \(t\) is minimized, whereas the hypograph lift \(t\leq f(x)\) is value-exact when \(t\) is maximized. Reversing either direction makes the lifted scalar objective unbounded when \(t\) has no independent bound. Neither one-sided set equals the graph: for every \(x\in K\), the epigraph contains every \(t>f(x)\), and the hypograph contains every \(t<f(x)\). Exact feasible-set representation of the graph therefore requires \(t=f(x)\), equivalently both inequalities. Additional constraints may also force this equality; an objective that forces equality only at optimal solutions can yield value exactness but does not make the entire feasible set graph-exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphs are value-exact for minimizing the lifted scalar and hypographs for maximizing it. A one-sided inequality does not encode the graph, even when the objective forces equality at optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: A scalar lift uses only one inequality, either \(t\geq f(x)\) or \(t\leq f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One-sided lifting is value-exact only with the matching optimization direction; exact graph representation requires both bounds, an equality, or other constraints that force equality throughout the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-to-Polynomial Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Denominator-safe polynomial graph lifting of a rational function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) on \(K\), where \(q(x)\neq0\) for every \(x\in K\). Introduce \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) and impose \(q(x)y-p(x)=0\). Then \(\{(x,y):x\in K,\ q(x)y-p(x)=0\}=\{(x,r(x)):x\in K\}\), so projection onto \(x\) recovers \(K\) and \(y\) uniquely records the rational value. Clearing denominators in inequalities additionally requires control of the sign of \(q\). If zeros of \(q\) are admitted, the polynomial equality may add points over a zero at which \(p\) also vanishes, so it need not represent the rational graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational graph becomes polynomial by enforcing denominator times value equals numerator, provided the denominator never vanishes; clearing denominators in inequalities additionally requires sign control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph of \(p/q\) over \(K\) equals \(\{(x,y):x\in K,\ q(x)y-p(x)=0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Semialgebraic-Function Graph Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential polynomial representation of graphs of semialgebraic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(f\) is semialgebraic, its graph \(\operatorname{gra}_K(f)\) is a semialgebraic subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\). Hence it admits a finite Boolean description by polynomial equalities and strict or weak inequalities. Equivalently, after introducing finitely many auxiliary variables \(z\in\mathbb{R}^r\) when needed to encode branches, one can choose finite polynomial families \(P_1,\ldots,P_a\), \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_b\), and \(R_1,\ldots,R_c\) such that \(\operatorname{gra}_K(f)=\{(x,y):\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ P_i(x,y,z)=0\ (i=1,\ldots,a),\ Q_j(x,y,z)\geq0\ (j=1,\ldots,b),\ R_\ell(x,y,z)>0\ (\ell=1,\ldots,c)\}\). The lifting is graph-exact precisely when its projection onto \((x,y)\) equals the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semialgebraic function has a semialgebraic graph, representable by finitely many polynomial sign conditions, possibly after adding variables to encode branches.
assumptions_latex: \(f:K\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is a semialgebraic function, meaning that its graph is semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are finitely many auxiliary variables and polynomial sign conditions whose projection onto \((x,y)\) is exactly \(\operatorname{gra}_K(f)\).

children.title: Polynomial Ideal Models

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Ideal Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained polynomial models encoded by a finitely generated ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equality constraints \(h_1(x)=\cdots=h_s(x)=0\), their polynomial ideal model is \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_s\rangle=\{\sum_{i=1}^s a_i h_i:a_i\in k[x]\}\). The associated algebraic feasible set is \(V_k(I)=\{u\in k^n:p(u)=0\text{ for every }p\in I\}\), which equals the common zero set of the generators. Replacing the generating list by another list that generates the same ideal leaves both the ideal model and its algebraic feasible set unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial equality constraints generate an ideal; its common zero set is the algebraic feasible set and is independent of the chosen generating list.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_s\rangle=\{\sum_{i=1}^s a_i h_i:a_i\in k[x]\}\) is the ideal model of the equality constraints.

notation.meaning: Polynomial ring in n variables over k.
Ideal generated by the equality polynomials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Discrete Domains from Zero-Dimensional Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-ideal representations of finite feasible domains in polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\geq0\ (j=1,\ldots,m_1),\ h_\ell(x)=0\ (\ell=1,\ldots,m_2)\}\) and \(J=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_{m_2}\rangle\). If \(J\) is zero dimensional, meaning that \(V_{\mathbb C}(J)\) is finite, then \(K\subseteq V_{\mathbb R}(J)\) is finite. For \(h_\ell(x)=x_\ell^2-x_\ell\), one has \(V_{\mathbb C}(J)=\{0,1\}^n\), and \(J\) is radical and real. More generally, if \(h_\ell(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{r_\ell}(x_\ell-x_{\ell j})\) for a finite set \(\{x_{\ell j}:j=1,\ldots,r_\ell\}\subset\mathbb R\), then \(V_{\mathbb C}(J)=\prod_{\ell=1}^n\{x_{\ell1},\ldots,x_{\ell r_\ell}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-dimensional equality ideal restricts the feasible set to finitely many points. Binary polynomial equations encode the Boolean cube, while coordinate polynomials with prescribed real roots encode finite Cartesian grids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is finite; the displayed equality systems encode }\{0,1\}^n\text{ and arbitrary finite Cartesian grids, respectively.}

children.title: Quotient-Ring Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial models represented through equivalence classes modulo an ideal.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Ring Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial expressions represented modulo equality consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quotient-ring model associated with \(I\) is \(R/I=\{f+I:f\in R\}\), with \([f]+[g]=[f+g]\) and \([f][g]=[fg]\). Equality \([f]=[g]\) holds if and only if \(f-g\in I\). Thus polynomial objectives and constraints may be represented by residue classes, identifying expressions that differ by an element of the equality ideal. For every \(u\in V_k(I)\), evaluation is well defined on residue classes because \(f-g\in I\) implies \(f(u)=g(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quotient ring identifies polynomials differing by an ideal element, so equality-constraint consequences become algebraic identities while evaluations on the variety remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a field, \(R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and \(I\subseteq R\) is an ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two polynomials represent the same element of \(R/I\) exactly when their difference lies in \(I\).

notation.meaning: Quotient ring of polynomial residue classes modulo I.
Residue class of f modulo I.
Zero set of the ideal I over k.

children.title: Reduction Modulo Polynomial Ideals
children.top_down_role: Model-level simplification of polynomial expressions using ideal relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Modulo Polynomial Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polynomial reduction using a fixed monomial order and a Gröbner basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f\in R\) and a Gröbner basis \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_s\}\) of \(I\), initialize \(p:=f\) and \(r:=0\). While \(p\neq0\), if some \(\operatorname{LM}(g_i)\) divides \(\operatorname{LM}(p)\), subtract from \(p\) a monomial multiple of \(g_i\) that cancels \(\operatorname{LT}(p)\); otherwise move \(\operatorname{LT}(p)\) from \(p\) to \(r\). When \(p=0\), output \(r=\operatorname{NF}_G(f)\). Then \(f-r\in I\), and no monomial of \(r\) is divisible by any \(\operatorname{LM}(g_i)\). For the fixed monomial order, this normal form is the unique reduced representative determined by the initial ideal and hence depends only on the residue class \([f]\in R/I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduce a polynomial by a Gröbner basis until no leading monomial is reducible; the resulting normal form represents its quotient-ring class.
assumptions_latex: \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_s\}\) is a Gröbner basis of an ideal \(I\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(f\in R\), the output \(r=\operatorname{NF}_G(f)\) satisfies \(f-r\in I\) and is the unique normal form of \([f]\in R/I\) for the fixed monomial order.

notation.meaning: Leading monomial under the fixed order.
Leading term under the fixed order.
Normal-form remainder of f modulo G.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonradical Ideal Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the nilpotent information retained by quotient models of nonradical polynomial ideals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k\) be a field and \(I\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) an ideal. The quotient algebra \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\) is reduced if and only if \(I\) is radical. Consequently, when \(I
e\sqrt I\), some \(f
otin I\) satisfies \(f^m\in I\) for an integer \(m\ge 2\); thus \([f]
e0\) is nilpotent in \(A\). Replacing \(I\) by \(\sqrt I\) preserves its algebraic zero set over an algebraic closure but removes nilpotents and therefore discards multiplicity or infinitesimal information encoded by the original quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonradical ideal produces nonzero nilpotents in its quotient ring. Radicalization preserves the algebraic zero set but can erase multiplicity information.

children.title: Variable-Elimination Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial representations obtained by removing designated variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Elimination Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents retained-variable consequences through an elimination ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a field, write variables as \((x,y)\in k^r\times k^s\), and let \(I=\langle h_1(x,y),\ldots,h_m(x,y)\rangle\subseteq k[x,y]\). Eliminating \(y\) produces the ideal \(I_x=I\cap k[x]\). Every feasible pair satisfying \(h_i(x,y)=0\) has retained coordinates satisfying \(g(x)=0\) for all \(g\in I_x\). If \(k\) is algebraically closed, then \(V(I_x)\) is exactly the Zariski closure of the coordinate projection of \(V(I)\); it need not equal the projection itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating variables means intersecting the original ideal with the retained-variable ring. Its variety describes the Zariski closure, not always the exact projection.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_r,y_1,\ldots,y_s]\) is generated by polynomial equations.
For the closure equality, \(k\) is algebraically closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_x=I\cap k[x]\) and \(V(I_x)=\overline{\pi_x(V(I))}^{\mathrm{Zar}}\).

notation.meaning: elimination ideal in the retained variables

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly distinguishes elimination consequences from exact projection, but the elimination/closure theorem has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Coordinate-Projection Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized around images of polynomial or semialgebraic sets in selected coordinates.

assumptions_latex: For the real projection statement, \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+s}\).
For the algebraic projection statement, \(k\) is algebraically closed and \(X\subseteq k^{r+s}\) is algebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^r:\exists y\in\mathbb R^s\text{ with }(x,y)\in S\}\); semialgebraic projections are semialgebraic, while projections of algebraic sets over \(k\) are constructible and need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a model obtained by retaining selected coordinates of an algebraic or semialgebraic feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+s}\) be a feasible set in variables \((x,y)\), and define \(\pi_x(x,y)=x\). Its coordinate-projection model is the retained-variable set
\[P=\pi_x(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^r:\exists y\in\mathbb R^s\text{ such that }(x,y)\in S\}.\]
If \(S\) is semialgebraic, then \(P\) is semialgebraic. Separately, if \(k\) is algebraically closed and \(X\subseteq k^{r+s}\) is algebraic, then \(\pi_x(X)\) is constructible and need not be algebraic or Zariski closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate-projection model retains selected variables and existentially quantifies the others. Real semialgebraic projections remain semialgebraic. Over an algebraically closed field, an algebraic projection is constructible but need not be algebraic or closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Volume and Exponential-Integrability Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes membership in the designated quasi-homogeneous polynomial class by exponential integrability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Scaling Formula for Quasi-Homogeneous Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents sublevel-set moments and volume using exponentially weighted integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $0<\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$, $g\in\mathbf{P}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathbf{u}}$, and $\mathbf{G}_y=\{\mathbf{x}:g(\mathbf{x})\le y\}$ for $y\ge0$. For every $\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n$, if $\int_{\mathbf{G}_y}\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\,d\mathbf{x}$ is finite, then
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbf{G}_y}\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\,d\mathbf{x}=\frac{y^{\sum_i u_i(1+\alpha_i)}}{\Gamma\!\left(1+\sum_i u_i(1+\alpha_i)\right)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}e^{-g(\mathbf{x})}\,d\mathbf{x}.$
In particular, with $|\mathbf{u}|=\sum_i u_i$,
$\displaystyle \operatorname{vol}(\mathbf{G}_y)=\frac{y^{|\mathbf{u}|}}{\Gamma(1+|\mathbf{u}|)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{-g(\mathbf{x})}\,d\mathbf{x}$ for $y\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite monomial moment over a nonnegative sublevel set of g equals a power of the level y, divided by a Gamma factor, times the corresponding exponentially weighted whole-space moment. Setting the monomial exponent to zero gives the volume formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_{\mathbf{G}_y}\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\,d\mathbf{x}=\frac{y^{\sum_i u_i(1+\alpha_i)}}{\Gamma\!\left(1+\sum_i u_i(1+\alpha_i)\right)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathbf{x}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}e^{-g(\mathbf{x})}\,d\mathbf{x},\quad \operatorname{vol}(\mathbf{G}_y)=\frac{y^{|\mathbf{u}|}}{\Gamma(1+|\mathbf{u}|)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{-g(\mathbf{x})}\,d\mathbf{x}

children.title: Projection Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Topological or algebraic boundary effects arising under coordinate projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes an exact algebraic projection from the variety defined by elimination equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Over an algebraically closed field \(k\), let \(I\subseteq k[x,y]\) and \(I_x=I\cap k[x]\). Then
\[\pi_x(V(I))\subseteq V(I_x)=\overline{\pi_x(V(I))}^{\mathrm{Zar}},\]
but the first inclusion may be strict. For example, with \(I=\langle xy-1\rangle\subseteq k[x,y]\), one has \(\pi_x(V(I))=k\setminus\{0\}\), while \(I_x=\{0\}\) and hence \(V(I_x)=k\). Thus elimination equations alone can add boundary points and cannot generally encode existential feasibility exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elimination describes the Zariski closure of a projection. The hyperbola xy=1 projects to nonzero x, although its elimination variety is the whole line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(I\cap k[x])=\overline{\pi_x(V(I))}^{\mathrm{Zar}}\), and equality with \(\pi_x(V(I))\) can fail.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement and hyperbola counterexample are mathematically appropriate, but the elimination closure theorem has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Fiber-Dimension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Projection models classified by the dimensions of eliminated-variable fibers.

knowledge_statements.title: Fiber-Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a dominant algebraic projection by its generic and exceptional fiber dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be irreducible algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field, and let \(\varphi:X\to Y\) be a dominant morphism. There exists a nonempty Zariski-open set \(U\subseteq Y\) such that every fiber over \(y\in U\) has dimension
\[\dim \varphi^{-1}(y)=\dim X-\dim Y.\]
For every \(y\in Y\), each nonempty fiber has dimension at least \(\dim X-\dim Y\). Hence zero-dimensional generic fibers describe generically finite elimination, whereas positive-dimensional generic fibers retain continuous families of eliminated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dominant projection has generic fiber dimension dim X minus dim Y; exceptional fibers may be larger. Zero-dimensional generic fibers correspond to generically finite elimination.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are irreducible varieties over an algebraically closed field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\varphi^{-1}(y)=\dim X-\dim Y\) on a nonempty open subset of \(Y\).

notation.meaning: fiber of the morphism over y

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly states the generic fiber-dimension regime under irreducibility, algebraic closedness, and dominance, but the fiber-dimension theorem requires an authoritative theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Reduced Coordinate Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents invariant polynomial models using generators of the invariant ring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly on \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) generate the invariant ring \(\mathbb R[x]^G\). Define the Hilbert map \(p(x)=(p_1(x),\ldots,p_m(x))\). Every invariant polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x]^G\) has a polynomial representative \(F\in\mathbb R[z_1,\ldots,z_m]\) satisfying \(f(x)=F(p(x))\). Therefore a \(G\)-invariant polynomial optimization model may be expressed in reduced coordinates \(z=p(x)\), provided the reduced feasible set includes the algebraic relations and real-orbit constraints defining \(p(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generators of the invariant ring provide reduced coordinates for symmetric polynomial models. Exact reformulation also requires constraints describing the attainable orbit-space image.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and acts linearly on \(\mathbb R^n\).
The objective and feasible set \(K\) are \(G\)-invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=F\circ p\) for every invariant polynomial \(f\), with reduced feasible region \(p(K)\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert map formed from invariant generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is locally appropriate and correctly notes that invariant generators alone do not describe the attainable real orbit space, but no invariant-theory or orbit-space source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Polynomial View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses polynomial optimization through finite coefficient vectors and monomial evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(d\in\mathbb N\), let \(\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}\) be the polynomials in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\), and index monomials by \(\mathcal A_d=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n:|\alpha|\le d\}\). Every \(f\in\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}\) is uniquely represented by a coefficient vector \(c=(c_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_d}\) with
\[f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_d}c_\alpha x^\alpha=\langle c,v_d(x)\rangle.\]
Thus a bounded-degree polynomial objective and constraints admit finite-dimensional coefficient representations, although optimization over their feasible point set may remain nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree polynomial is a finite coefficient vector paired with the monomial vector. This gives a finite-dimensional model but does not remove nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}\cong\mathbb R^{\binom{n+d}{d}}\) through the monomial coefficient map.

notation.meaning: multi-indices of total degree at most d
vector of monomials indexed by \(\mathcal A_d\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial optimization over a basic closed semialgebraic set

The polynomial optimization problem has value \(f^*:=\inf\{f(\mathbf x):\mathbf x\in\mathbf K\}\). A set defined by finitely many polynomial inequalities of this form is called a basic closed semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For real polynomials f and g_1 through g_m, the problem minimizes f over points satisfying g_j(x) ≥ 0 for every j. A set defined by finitely many such nonstrict polynomial inequalities is a basic closed semialgebraic set.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Moment Problem View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recasts compact polynomial minimization as linear optimization over probability measures and their moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). With \(\mathcal P(K)\) denoting Borel probability measures supported on \(K\),
\[\min_{x\in K}f(x)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(K)}\int_K f(x)\,d\mu(x).\]
Writing \(y_\alpha=\int_Kx^\alpha\,d\mu\), the right side is the linear objective \(\sum_\alpha f_\alpha y_\alpha\), subject to \(y_0=1\) and the requirement that \(y\) admit a representing measure supported on \(K\). An optimal Dirac measure is supported at any global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial minimization on a compact set equals linear minimization over supported probability measures, with objective linear in the measure's moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in K}f(x)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(K)}\int_K f\,d\mu\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures supported on K
moment indexed by the multi-index alpha

children.title: Copositive Cone View
children.top_down_role: High-level polynomial model interfaces expressed through copositive cone structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Copositive Cone View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the matrix cone whose quadratic forms are nonnegative on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb N\), the copositive cone is
\[\operatorname{COP}_n=\{A\in\mathbb S^n:x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R_+^n\}.\]
It is a closed convex cone. Unlike the positive-semidefinite cone, its defining inequality is imposed only on the nonnegative orthant. Consequently, a homogeneous quadratic polynomial \(q_A(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax\) is nonnegative on \(\mathbb R_+^n\) if and only if its symmetric coefficient matrix \(A\) belongs to \(\operatorname{COP}_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is copositive when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every nonnegative vector. These matrices form a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\in\operatorname{COP}_n\iff x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge0\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and closed-convex-cone property fit the copositive-cone terminal, but no source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Completely Positive Cone View
children.top_down_role: High-level polynomial model interfaces expressed through completely positive cone structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Completely Positive Cone View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cone generated by rank-one matrices formed from nonnegative vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb N\), the completely positive cone is
\[\operatorname{CP}_n=\left\{X\in\mathbb S^n:X=\sum_{j=1}^r v_jv_j^{\mathsf T}\text{ for some }r\in\mathbb N\text{ and }v_j\in\mathbb R_+^n\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(X\in\operatorname{CP}_n\) if and only if \(X=BB^{\mathsf T}\) for some entrywise nonnegative matrix \(B\) with finitely many columns. The cone \(\operatorname{CP}_n\) is convex and closed and consists of positive-semidefinite, entrywise nonnegative matrices, although the converse fails in general dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is completely positive when it factors as BBᵀ with B entrywise nonnegative, equivalently as a finite sum of nonnegative rank-one matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\operatorname{CP}_n\iff X=BB^{\mathsf T}\) for some entrywise nonnegative finite matrix \(B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and finite nonnegative factorization are standard, but the claim that the doubly-nonnegative converse fails should specify the dimension regime, and all cone properties require an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Primal–Dual Cone Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representation-level pairing between the two cone-based model views.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Cone Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States trace-inner-product duality between completely positive and copositive matrix cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(\mathbb S^n\) with the trace inner product \(\langle A,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AX)\). Then the completely positive and copositive cones are mutually dual:
\[\operatorname{CP}_n^*=\operatorname{COP}_n,\qquad \operatorname{COP}_n^*=\operatorname{CP}_n.\]
Indeed, for \(X=\sum_jv_jv_j^{\mathsf T}\) with \(v_j\ge0\), one has \(\langle A,X\rangle=\sum_jv_j^{\mathsf T}Av_j\). Thus \(A\) pairs nonnegatively with every completely positive matrix exactly when its quadratic form is nonnegative on \(\mathbb R_+^n\); the reverse equality follows from closedness and bipolar duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the trace inner product, the dual of the completely positive cone is the copositive cone, and conversely.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) carries the inner product \(\langle A,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AX)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CP}_n^*=\operatorname{COP}_n\) and \(\operatorname{COP}_n^*=\operatorname{CP}_n\).

notation.meaning: dual cone under the trace inner product

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mutual cone-duality claim has the correct mathematical role and hypotheses, but no authoritative locator is supplied. The sentences beginning with 'Indeed' and invoking bipolar duality are proof text and should be removed when the sourced record is resubmitted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value and disintegration of the joint-marginal optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the optimal value and optimal measures, including the almost-everywhere unique-minimizer regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf Y\subset\mathbb R^p\) and \(\mathbf K\subset\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be compact, let \(\varphi\) be the prescribed probability measure from the joint-marginal formulation, and assume \(\mathbf K_{\mathbf y}\neq\varnothing\) for every \(\mathbf y\in\mathbf Y\). Then the joint-marginal problem attains its optimum and \(\rho=\int_{\mathbf Y}J(\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\). Every optimal \(\mu^*\) admits a disintegration \(\mu^*(C\times B)=\int_B\psi^*(C\mid\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\), where \(\psi^*(\cdot\mid\mathbf y)\) is concentrated on \(\mathbf X^*(\mathbf y)\) for \(\varphi\)-almost every \(\mathbf y\). If \(\mathbf X^*(\mathbf y)=\{\mathbf x^*(\mathbf y)\}\) almost everywhere, there is a measurable \(g:\mathbf Y\to\mathbb R^n\) equal to \(\mathbf x^*(\mathbf y)\) almost everywhere, and for all \(\alpha\in\mathbb N^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb N^p\), \(\int_{\mathbf K}\mathbf x^\alpha\mathbf y^\beta\,d\mu^*=\int_{\mathbf Y}\mathbf y^\beta g(\mathbf y)^\alpha\,d\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The joint-marginal problem attains the average of the pointwise optimal values. Its optimal measures disintegrate into conditional measures supported on pointwise minimizers. Almost-everywhere uniqueness yields a measurable optimizer selection and the corresponding moment identities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual SOS hierarchy for parametric polynomial value-function underapproximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOS dual of the joint-marginal moment relaxation, including degree restrictions and its relation to unrestricted polynomial underestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual of the order-\(d\) moment relaxation is \(\rho_d^*=\sup_{p_d,(\sigma_j)}\int_{\mathbf Y}p_d\,d\varphi=\sup\sum_{\beta\in\mathbb N^p_{2d}}p_{d\beta}\gamma_\beta\), subject to \(f-p_d=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^t\sigma_jh_j\), where \(p_d\in\mathbb R[\mathbf y]\), the \(\sigma_j\) are sums of squares in \((\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\), \(\deg p_d\le2d\), and \(\deg(\sigma_jh_j)\le2d\) for \(j=1,\ldots,t\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: The construction of the surrogate polynomials and the hypotheses of Theorem 14.5 are incorporated by reference because the extract does not restate them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf\Omega\subseteq\mathbf Y\), assume the hypotheses of Theorem 14.5, and let \(p_d\in\mathbb R[\mathbf y]\) be defined as in Theorem 14.6(b). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inverse polynomial optimization problem for the observation \(\bar x\) is \[\inf_{c\in C}\ d(c,c^0)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_c(\bar x)\le f_c(x)\ \text{for every }x\in K,\] where \(f_c(x):=\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_\alpha x^\alpha\). The universal inequality is equivalent to \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f_c(x).\] Thus the decision variables are objective coefficients, while \(K\) and \(\bar x\) are data; additional normalization constraints in \(C\) may exclude trivial objectives such as \(f_c\equiv 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse polynomial optimization adjusts objective coefficients so an observed feasible point becomes globally optimal, while remaining close to nominal coefficients.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Polynomial Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-inference formulation fits inverse polynomial optimization and definition is the correct knowledge kind. No authoritative source is supplied, and the assumptions do not specify the codomain or basic admissibility properties of the discrepancy function d needed to make the optimization objective well-defined.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree-bounded Putinar certificate of global optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an SOS certificate for a candidate optimizer of a polynomial over a basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf y\in\mathbf K\) and \(h\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]\). If there exist \(\sigma_j\in\Sigma[\mathbf x]_d\), \(j=0,\ldots,m\), such that \[h(\mathbf x)-h(\mathbf y)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sigma_j(\mathbf x)g_j(\mathbf x)\qquad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n,\] then this identity is called a Putinar certificate of global optimality on \(\mathbf K\), with degree bound \(d\), for \(\mathbf y\) and \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For y in K and a polynomial h, an identity expressing h(x)-h(y) as a sum of SOS weights times the defining polynomials g_j, valid for every x in R^n and using SOS weights of degree bound d, is a Putinar certificate of global optimality on K for y and h.
assumptions_latex: \exists\,\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_m\in\Sigma[\mathbf x]_d:\ h(\mathbf x)-h(\mathbf y)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sigma_j(\mathbf x)g_j(\mathbf x)\quad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h(\mathbf x)-h(\mathbf y)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sigma_j(\mathbf x)g_j(\mathbf x)\text{ is a degree-}d\text{ Putinar certificate of global optimality on }\mathbf K\text{ for }(\mathbf y,h).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No duality gap and primal attainment for inverse-polynomial SDPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded result for the three specified primal-dual SDP pairs arising from the inverse polynomial formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\mathbf K\subset\mathbb R^n\) has nonempty interior. Then there is no duality gap between \((16.5)\) and \((16.8)\), between \((16.6)\) and \((16.9)\), and between \((16.7)\) and \((16.10)\). Moreover, each of the primal programs \((16.5)\), \((16.6)\), and \((16.7)\) has an optimal solution \(\widetilde f_d\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]_{d_0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If K has nonempty interior, each specified inverse-polynomial primal-dual SDP pair has no duality gap, and each of the three primal SDPs attains an optimal polynomial solution of degree at most d_0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gap}(16.5,16.8)=\operatorname{gap}(16.6,16.9)=\operatorname{gap}(16.7,16.10)=0,\quad (16.5),(16.6),(16.7)\text{ each attain an optimizer }\widetilde f_d\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]_{d_0}.
